Generators and Lefschetz properties of general hyperplane arrangement apolar algebras

Date: 25 October 2026
Abstract.

Hyperplane arrangements are rich combinatorial, topological, and geometric objects with numerous applications. Apolarity is a method of turning a homogeneous polynomial into a finite graded Gorenstein algebra. Invariants of the apolar algebra of the defining equation of a hyperplane arrangement are invariants of the arrangement itself. We investigate such invariants, including the Hilbert function, minimal generators of the apolar ideal, and Lefschetz properties. The main focus of the article is on combinatorially general arrangements of degree dd in dimension nn with n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. In this range, we determine the Hilbert function and conjecture that the same formula is valid for larger values of dd too. Minimal generators of the apolar ideal in the initial degree are in natural bijection to the lines of the arrangement. The initial degree characterizes arrangements that are combinatorially general. Finally, we prove that the apolar algebra has the Weak Lefschetz Property and precisely characterize the Weak Lefschetz elements.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14N20; Secondary 13H10, 13A02, 13A15

1. Introduction

Throughout the article we work over a field 𝕜\Bbbk of characteristic 00 or sufficiently large. Let S=𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}] and T=𝕜⁡[α1,…,αn]T=\Bbbk[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}], and let elements of TT act as differential operators on SS, with αi\alpha_{i} acting as ∂/∂xi\partial/\partial x_{i}. For a homogeneous polynomial F∈S=𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]F\in S=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}], the apolar ideal or annihilator ideal is the ideal Ann⁡(F)⊆T\Ann(F)\subseteq T consisting of elements that annihilate FF. For example, if F=x1d1​⋯​xndnF=x_{1}^{d_{1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{d_{n}} is a monomial, then Ann⁡(F)=(α1d1+1,…,αndn+1)\Ann(F)=(\alpha_{1}^{d_{1}+1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}^{d_{n}+1}). The apolar algebra of FF is the quotient T/Ann⁡(F)T/\Ann(F).

Apolarity arises in connection to a number of topics, for example:

  • •

    finite local algebras (primarily those that are in addition Gorenstein) [21], [24], [9], [12],

  • •

    Waring and tensor rank decompositions, and their many variants [8], [7], [16], [6], [3],

  • •

    secant varieties [5], and

  • •

    interesting examples of special varieties such as K​3K3-surfaces [23], Fano 33-folds [34], [26] or hyperkähler 4-folds [35].

In this note we consider a special class of polynomials, the completely reducible ones, meaning polynomials that factor as a product of linear factors. These are the defining equations of hyperplane arrangements. The apolar ideals and algebras are well understood for the equations of only a few extremely special families of arrangements. We have mentioned monomials. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the arrangement of mirror hyperplanes of a finite reflection group, then the apolar ideal of the equation of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the ideal generated by the positive-degree coinvariants of the arrangement; see for example [28, Chapter 26]. Apolarity of binary forms is well understood, and (over a closed field) these are completely reducible. Beyond these, there are not any other families of hyperplane arrangements whose apolarity has been worked out. Individual examples are easy to compute.

Some prior work on apolarity of arrangements has investigated whether apolarity is combinatorial, or, in other words, whether certain invariants of apolarity, such as the Hilbert function of the apolar algebra, are determined by the intersection lattice of the arrangement. Another problem that has been studied is that of determining which arrangements have an apolar algebra that is a complete intersection. Mirror arrangements of finite reflection groups have complete intersection apolar algebras, but many other arrangements do not.

Wakefield’s thesis [40] presents two arrangements with isomorphic intersection lattices where the apolar algebra of one arangement is a complete intersection, but the apolar algebra of the other is not [40, Example III.4.3, Example III.5.1]. Wakefield conjectures that, for a general arrangement (one whose hyperplanes are in general position) with degree n+1⩽d<∞n+1\leqslant d<\infty, its apolar algebra is not a complete intersection [40, Conjecture III.3.3]. Subsequently, DiPasquale–Flores–Peterson gave a lower bound for the initial degree of the apolar ideal of an arrangement that is combinatorially general (one whose hyperplanes are as independent as possible, see Definition 2.2 below) [11, Proposition 4.10]. They use this to prove Wakefield’s conjecture in the range of degrees n+1⩽d⩽(n−1)​nn+1\leqslant d\leqslant(n-1)n [11, Corollary 4.11].

In a different direction, Garoussian–Tohǎneanu used apolarity of arrangements to investigate codes [17, Section 3.1].

In this note we consider a hyperplane arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} with defining equation FF. We are able to work out a fairly complete picture of their apolarity, starting with the Hilbert function of the apolar algebra AF=T/Ann⁡(F)A^{F}=T/\Ann(F) for a general arrangement.

Theorem 1.1.

Assume that the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let F=ℓ1​ℓ2​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dotsm\ell_{d} with ℓi∈𝕜⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\ell_{i}\in\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},\dotsc,x_{n}] general linear forms. If n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2, then the Hilbert function of AFA^{F} is given by

dimAkF={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽d−n+1(dk),d−n+1⩽k⩽n−1(n−1+d−kd−k),n−1⩽k⩽d\dim A^{F}_{k}=\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1\\ \binom{d}{k},&d-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&n-1\leqslant k\leqslant d\end{cases}

If d=2​n−1d=2n-1, the Hilbert function is given by

dimAkF={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽n−1(n−1+d−kd−k),n⩽k⩽d\dim A^{F}_{k}=\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant n-1\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&n\leqslant k\leqslant d\end{cases}

This is a simplified version of Theorem 3.14, which in particular provides more precise genericity conditions on the arrangement. We conjecture that for degrees d>2​n−1d>2n-1, the Hilbert function is given by the same expression, see Conjecture 6.1.

We are further able to bound the minimal degree of an element of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F).

Theorem 1.2.

Assume the characteristic of the field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let F=ℓ1​ℓ2​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dotsm\ell_{d} with ℓi∈𝕜⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\ell_{i}\in\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},\dotsc,x_{n}] pairwise nonproportional linear forms, representing an arbitrary reduced central hyperplane arrangement. The minimal degree of a nonzero element of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is less than or equal to d−n+2d-n+2.

Assume n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. Then equality holds in the above bound for the minimal degree if and only if the arrangement is combinatorially general, i.e., represents the uniform matroid (see Definition 2.2).

The proof follows from Theorem 4.3.

For products of general linear forms of certain specific degrees, we describe the degrees of a minimal generating set for Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F).

Theorem 1.3.

Fix integers n,dn,d. Assume the characteristic of the field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let F=ℓ1​ℓ2​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dotsm\ell_{d} with ℓi∈𝕜⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\ell_{i}\in\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},\dotsc,x_{n}] general linear forms. If n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 then the apolar ideal Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is minimally generated in degrees d−n+2d-n+2 and nn, with (dn−1)\binom{d}{n-1} generators in degree d−n+2d-n+2 and (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} generators in degree nn. If d−n+2=nd-n+2=n, equivalently d=2​n−2d=2n-2, then Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is minimally generated by (dn−1)+(d−1n)\binom{d}{n-1}+\binom{d-1}{n} generators in degree d−n+2=nd-n+2=n.

See Theorem 4.7 for more details, including the precise genericity conditions and explicit construction of the minimal generators in degree d−n+2d-n+2.

Furthermore, we discuss the problem of Lefschetz properties of AFA^{F}. A finite standard graded algebra A=A0⊕⋯⊕AdA=A_{0}\oplus\dotsb\oplus A_{d} has the weak Lefschetz property if for a general α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1}, for every ii, the multiplication map α:Ai→Ai+1\alpha\colon A_{i}\to A_{i+1}, Θ↦α​Θ\Theta\mapsto\alpha\Theta, has full rank, that is, it is either injective or surjective.

Theorem 1.4.

Assume the characteristic of the field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let F=ℓ1​ℓ2​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dotsm\ell_{d} with ℓi∈𝕜⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]\ell_{i}\in\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},\dotsc,x_{n}] general linear forms. If n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 then AFA^{F} has the Weak Lefschetz Property. An element α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1} satisfies the Weak Lefschetz condition if and only if α\alpha lies in a certain explicitly described locus.

This is the simplified version of Theorem 5.8, which also specifies the generality conditions on ℓi\ell_{i} and describes which linear forms α\alpha satisfy the Weak Lefschetz condition (see Definition 5.1).

2. Arrangements, apolarity, and Gorenstein symmetries

We review some basic notions of hyperplane arrangements and apolarity.

2.1. Hyperplane arrangements

For an overview, definitions, and many properties of arrangements see [10] or [32]. We recall some basic definitions and terminology here.

Definition 2.1.

An affine hyperplane arrangement 𝒜={H1,…,Hd}\mathcal{A}=\{H_{1},\dotsc,H_{d}\} is a finite set of affine hyperplanes in affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over a field 𝕜\Bbbk, a priori allowing repetition (multiplicity). We identify 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the union of the HiH_{i}. That is, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a hypersurface defined by a polynomial FF that factors into linear factors, F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d} where the ℓi\ell_{i} are linear forms defined over 𝕜\Bbbk. A hyperplane arrangement is central if every hyperplane passes through the origin, or equivalently if each ℓi\ell_{i} is a homogeneous linear form, or equivalently if FF is homogeneous. A hyperplane arrangement is reduced or simple if the factors ℓi\ell_{i} are pairwise nonproportional, or equivalently if they define pairwise distinct hyperplanes.

Throughout this paper we only consider central reduced hyperplane arrangements. For brevity we may simply say arrangement.

An arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} (central, reduced) of degree dd represents the matroid M𝒜M_{\mathcal{A}} on the ground set [d]={1,…,d}[d]=\{1,\dotsc,d\}, where a subset I⊆[d]I\subseteq[d] is independent if the hyperplanes indexed by II intersect transversally, so that codim⋂i∈IHi=#I\codim\bigcap_{i\in I}H_{i}=\#I.

Definition 2.2.

An arrangement is combinatorially general if, for all rr, every rr hyperplanes of the arrangement intersect in codimension min⁡{r,n}\min\{r,n\}.

For an arrangement to be combinatorially general, it is equivalent to say that the arrangement represents the uniform matroid of rank nn, which is the matroid in which every set of rr elements is independent if and only if r⩽nr\leqslant n.

Remark 2.3.

Some references, for instance [10, Def. 2.18], [32, Def. 5.22] use the term generic instead of combinatorially general. However the term “generic” has a special meaning in algebraic geometry, so we prefer to use the term “combinatorially general”. The authors of [18] use the term meets properly to describe such an arrangement. It is equivalent to say that the associated projective arrangement has normal crossings.

Definition 2.4.

A property PP holds for a general arrangement if it holds for all arrangements in some dense Zariski open subset of the space parametrizing arrangements.

The combinatorially general arrangements are a dense open subset of the arrangements. In particular, a property that holds for combinatorially general arrangements certainly holds for a general arrangement. Conversely, a property that holds for a general arrangement does not necessarily hold for every combinatorially general arrangement.

For a concrete example where a combinatorially general arrangement exhibits non-general behavior, see section 6.1.

2.2. Apolarity

Definition 2.5.

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be an arbitrary field. Let S=𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}] and T=𝕜⁡[α1,…,αn]T=\Bbbk[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}] be polynomial rings; we say SS is the (ordinary) polynomial ring and TT is the (graded) dual ring. We regard SS as a TT-module where αi\alpha_{i} acts as the partial differentiation operator ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}. We denote this action by   \mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}, so that αi  F=∂∂xi​F\alpha_{i}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}F for F∈SF\in S.

For F∈SF\in S let Derivs⁡(F)⊂S\Derivs(F)\subset S, the space of derivatives of FF, be the 𝕜\Bbbk-vector subspace spanned by all the derivatives of FF of all orders, including FF itself. It is a TT-submodule of SS. When FF is homogeneous, Derivs⁡(F)\Derivs(F) is graded by degree. We write Derivs⁡(F)k\Derivs(F)_{k} for the subspace of derivatives of degree kk, equivalently the (d−k)(d-k)th derivatives where d=deg⁡Fd=\deg F.

The apolar ideal or annihilator ideal of FF is Ann(F)=(0:F)={Θ∈T:Θ  F=0}⊆T\Ann(F)=(0:F)=\{\Theta\in T:\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=0\}\subseteq T. When FF is homogeneous, Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is a homogeneous ideal. For a subspace P⊆SP\subseteq S, Ann⁡(P)=⋂F∈PAnn⁡(F)\Ann(P)=\bigcap_{F\in P}\Ann(F), and this is a homogeneous ideal if PP is spanned by homogeneous forms.

For fixed FF, the evaluation map T→ST\to S given by Θ↦Θ  F\Theta\mapsto\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F is 𝕜\Bbbk-linear and in fact a map of TT-modules, with image Derivs⁡(F)\Derivs(F) and kernel Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F). (This is essentially the catalecticant of FF, although that name is usually used just for the maps of graded pieces Td−k→SkT_{d-k}\to S_{k}, and in fact even just for the matrices representing those maps.)

The apolar algebra is AF=T/Ann⁡(F)A^{F}=T/\Ann(F). It is an Artinian Gorenstein 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra of socle degree dd. See [22, Def. 1.11], [25, Thm 3.26] and references therein.

For any graded object MM we write MdM_{d} for the graded piece of MM of degree dd. We may identify S1S_{1} with T1∗T_{1}^{*}. Polynomials F∈SF\in S are naturally functions T1→𝕜T_{1}\to\Bbbk.

Lemma 2.6.

Assume 𝕜\Bbbk has characteristic zero or strictly greater than dd. Let F∈SdF\in S_{d} be a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd. For α∈T1\alpha\in T_{1}, αd  F=d!​F​(α)\alpha^{d}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=d!F(\alpha).

This is well-known; see for example [13, Proposition 3.1], [22, Lemma 1.15(1)], [36, (1.5)]. It can be directly verified when FF is monomial using the multinomial theorem, or even more simply when FF is a power of a linear form, and then extended to all FF by linearity.

Almost equally well known is the following. For example, it appears in [29, Proposition 6.3], but was doubtlessly familiar long before that.

2.3. Gorenstein symmetries

Let A=AF=T/Ann⁡(F)A=A^{F}=T/\Ann(F) be the apolar algebra of a homogeneous form FF of degree dd in nn variables.

The Hilbert function of AA is symmetric:

Lemma 2.9.

For all ii, dimAi=dimAd−i\dim A_{i}=\dim A_{d-i}, and equivalently, dimDerivs⁡(F)i=dimDerivs⁡(F)d−i\dim\Derivs(F)_{i}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{d-i}.

In fact, the spaces AiA_{i} and Ad−iA_{d-i}, and the graded pieces of Derivs⁡(F)\Derivs(F), have a natural pairing:

Lemma 2.10.

For all ii, the bilinear map Ai×Ad−i→Ad≅𝕜A_{i}\times A_{d-i}\to A_{d}\cong\Bbbk given by (θ,ψ)↦θ​ψ  F(\theta,\psi)\mapsto\theta\psi\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F is a perfect pairing, that is, the induced maps Ai→Ad−i∗A_{i}\to A_{d-i}^{*} and Ad−i→Ai∗A_{d-i}\to A_{i}^{*} are isomorphisms.

Likewise the bilinear map Derivs⁡(F)i×Derivs⁡(F)d−i→Derivs⁡(F)0≅𝕜\Derivs(F)_{i}\times\Derivs(F)_{d-i}\to\Derivs(F)_{0}\cong\Bbbk given by (g,h)=(θ  F,ψ  F)↦θ​ψ  F(g,h)=(\theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F,\psi\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F)\mapsto\theta\psi\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F is well defined and a perfect pairing.

Finally the bilinear map Ai×Derivs⁡(F)i→Derivs⁡(F)0≅𝕜A_{i}\times\Derivs(F)_{i}\to\Derivs(F)_{0}\cong\Bbbk given by (θ,g)↦θ  g(\theta,g)\mapsto\theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}g is a perfect pairing. In particular, for α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1}, the multiplication map α:Ai→Ai+1\alpha:A_{i}\to A_{i+1} and the differentiation map α  :Derivs(F)i+1→Derivs(F)i\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}:\Derivs(F)_{i+1}\to\Derivs(F)_{i} are adjoint (transpose).

More interestingly, the minimal graded free resolution of AA as a TT-module is symmetric. For a graded TT-module MM, let M∗=HomT⁡(M,T)M^{*}=\Hom_{T}(M,T) be the graded module consisting of graded TT-module homomorphisms from MM to TT.

Lemma 2.11.

Let 0→Mc→⋯→M1→M0=T→00\to M_{c}\to\dotsb\to M_{1}\to M_{0}=T\to 0 be the minimal graded free resolution of AA as a TT-module. Then the length of the resolution is c=nc=n, and 0→M0∗​(−d−n)→M1∗​(−d−n)→⋯→Mc∗​(−d−n)→00\to M_{0}^{*}(-d-n)\to M_{1}^{*}(-d-n)\to\dotsb\to M_{c}^{*}(-d-n)\to 0 is isomorphic to the first resolution. In particular the graded Betti numbers satisfy βi,j=βn−i,d+n−j\beta_{i,j}=\beta_{n-i,d+n-j}.

While these statements are well-known, we found it surprisingly difficult to locate clear references, especially for the precise value of the shift appearing in the self-duality of the resolution. For completeness, we provide proofs of these statements in Appendix A.

3. Hilbert function of combinatorially general arrangements

In this section we determine the Hilbert function of the apolar algebra AFA^{F} when FF is the defining equation of a combinatorially general arrangement of degree dd and dimension nn, where dd satisfies n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2.

3.1. Spaces of products

Definition 3.1.

Given an arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} in 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n} with defining equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}, for each k⩾0k\geqslant 0, let products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} be the set of products of any kk of the ℓi\ell_{i}. In notation,

products⁡(F)k={ℓi1​⋯​ℓik:1⩽i1<⋯<ik⩽d}.\products(F)_{k}=\{\ell_{i_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{i_{k}}\colon 1\leqslant i_{1}<\dotsb<i_{k}\leqslant d\}.

Note products⁡(F)0={1}\products(F)_{0}=\{1\}. Let products⁡(F)\products(F) be the union of the sets products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} over all kk.

Let Products⁡(F)⊂S\Products(F)\subset S be the 𝕜\Bbbk-vector space spanned by products of subsets of the ℓi\ell_{i}, including FF itself and 11, the empty product. It is graded by degree, with Products⁡(F)k\Products(F)_{k} spanned by products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k}.

Observe that Derivs⁡(F)k⊆Products⁡(F)k⊆Sk\Derivs(F)_{k}\subseteq\Products(F)_{k}\subseteq S_{k} for each kk. From these containments and Lemma 2.9 we obtain the inequalities

(3.2) dimDerivs⁡(F)k⩽min⁡{dimSk,dimProducts⁡(F)k,dimTd−k}⩽min⁡{(n−1+kk),(dk),(n−1+d−kd−k)}.\begin{split}\dim\Derivs(F)_{k}&\leqslant\min\{\dim S_{k},\dim\Products(F)_{k},\dim T_{d-k}\}\\ &\leqslant\min\left\{\binom{n-1+k}{k},\binom{d}{k},\binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k}\right\}.\end{split}
Lemma 3.3.

For n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 and 0⩽k⩽d0\leqslant k\leqslant d,

(3.4) min⁡{(n−1+kk),(dk),(n−1+d−kd−k)}={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽d−n+1(dk),d−n+1⩽k⩽n−1(n−1+d−kd−k),n−1⩽k⩽d\min\left\{\binom{n-1+k}{k},\binom{d}{k},\binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k}\right\}\\ =\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1\\ \binom{d}{k},&d-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&n-1\leqslant k\leqslant d\\ \end{cases}

For 2​n−1⩽d2n-1\leqslant d and 0⩽k⩽d0\leqslant k\leqslant d,

(3.5) min⁡{(n−1+kk),(dk),(n−1+d−kd−k)}={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽⌊d2⌋(n−1+d−kd−k),⌈d2⌉⩽k⩽d\min\left\{\binom{n-1+k}{k},\binom{d}{k},\binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k}\right\}\\ =\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil\leqslant k\leqslant d\\ \end{cases}
Proof.

Direct calculation. ∎

The goal of this section is to prove that the Hilbert function of the apolar algebra of a combinatorially general arrangement is given exactly by the expressions of Lemma 3.3, at least when n⩽d⩽2​n−1n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-1.

Remark 3.6.

Recall that a sequence (a0,…,ad)(a_{0},\dotsc,a_{d}) is symmetric if ak=ad−ka_{k}=a_{d-k} for all kk, unimodal if a0⩽a1⩽⋯⩽am⩾⋯⩾ada_{0}\leqslant a_{1}\leqslant\dotsb\leqslant a_{m}\geqslant\dotsb\geqslant a_{d} for some mm, and log-concave if ak2⩾ak−1​ak+1a_{k}^{2}\geqslant a_{k-1}a_{k+1} for all 1⩽k⩽d−11\leqslant k\leqslant d-1 (assuming that the aka_{k} are nonnegative).

The sequences defined in Lemma 3.3 are clearly unimodal and symmetric. In addition, they are minimums of log-concave sequences; hence they are also log-concave.

First we describe the Hilbert function of Products⁡(F)\Products(F).

Lemma 3.7.

For 0⩽m⩽n0\leqslant m\leqslant n, ∑i=0m(nm−i)​(x−1)i=∑i=0m(n−i−1m−i)​xi\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{n}{m-i}(x-1)^{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{n-i-1}{m-i}x^{i}.

Proof.

First expand the right hand side using xi=((x−1)+1)ix^{i}=((x-1)+1)^{i} and interchange the order of summation:

∑i=0m(n−i−1m−1)​xi=∑j=0m∑i=jm(n−i−1m−i)​(ij)​(x−1)j.\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{n-i-1}{m-1}x^{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sum_{i=j}^{m}\binom{n-i-1}{m-i}\binom{i}{j}(x-1)^{j}.

Now recall the Chu–Vandermonde-type identity ∑k(a−kp)​(kq)=(a+1p+q+1)\sum_{k}\binom{a-k}{p}\binom{k}{q}=\binom{a+1}{p+q+1}. (The left hand side counts the number of ways to choose a subset of {1,…,a+1}\{1,\dotsc,a+1\} by choosing a value k+1k+1, then choosing pp values strictly greater than k+1k+1 and qq values less than or equal to kk.) Applying this gives

∑i=jm(n−i−1m−i)​(ij)=∑i=jm(n−i−1n−m−1)​(ij)=(nn−m+j)=(nm−j),\sum_{i=j}^{m}\binom{n-i-1}{m-i}\binom{i}{j}=\sum_{i=j}^{m}\binom{n-i-1}{n-m-1}\binom{i}{j}=\binom{n}{n-m+j}=\binom{n}{m-j},

as claimed. ∎

The next lemma is essentially equivalent to Proposition 3.5 of [39], but the proof there is only for characteristic zero.

Lemma 3.8.

Let F∈SdF\in S_{d} be the defining equation of a hyperplane arrangement of degree dd in dimension nn, with n⩽dn\leqslant d. Assume that the arrangement is combinatorially general. The sets products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} have maximal rank in the sense that for each kk, either products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} spans SkS_{k}, or it is linearly independent. Explicitly, for 0⩽k⩽d−n+10\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1, products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} spans SkS_{k}, and for d−n+1⩽k⩽dd-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant d, the products in products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} are linearly independent. Thus for 0⩽k⩽d−n+10\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1, dimProducts⁡(F)k=dimSk=(n−1+kk)\dim\Products(F)_{k}=\dim S_{k}=\binom{n-1+k}{k}, and for d−n+1⩽k⩽dd-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant d, dimProducts⁡(F)k=(dk)\dim\Products(F)_{k}=\binom{d}{k}.

Proof.

Berget [2, Corollary 3.1] shows that the Hilbert series of Products⁡(F)\Products(F) is given by a Tutte polynomial evaluation as follows. For an arbitrary arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} with defining equation GG, say with dd hyperplanes in nn dimensions, with d⩾nd\geqslant n,

∑k=0d(dimProducts⁡(G)k)​tk=td−n​T𝒜​(1+t,t−1)\sum_{k=0}^{d}(\dim\Products(G)_{k})t^{k}=t^{d-n}T_{\mathcal{A}}(1+t,t^{-1})

where T𝒜T_{\mathcal{A}} is the Tutte polynomial of the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A}, or equivalently its matroid.

In our case, the arrangement is combinatorially general, which means that its matroid is the uniform matroid of rank nn on dd elements. Directly by definition, the Tutte polynomial of this arrangement is

T𝒜​(q,t)=∑k=0n−1(dk)​(q−1)n−k+∑k=nd(dk)​(t−1)k−n=∑k=0n−1(dk)​(q−1)n−k+∑k=nd(n−1+d−kd−k)​tk−n,\begin{split}T_{\mathcal{A}}(q,t)&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{d}{k}(q-1)^{n-k}+\sum_{k=n}^{d}\binom{d}{k}(t-1)^{k-n}\\ &=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{d}{k}(q-1)^{n-k}+\sum_{k=n}^{d}\binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k}t^{k-n},\end{split}

by substitution in Lemma 3.8. We evaluate

td−n​T𝒜​(1+t,t−1)=∑k=0n−1(dk)​td−k+∑k=nd(n−1+d−kd−k)​td−k=∑k=0d−n(n−1+kk)​tk+∑k=d−n+1d(dk)​tk.\begin{split}t^{d-n}T_{\mathcal{A}}(1+t,t^{-1})&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{d}{k}t^{d-k}+\sum_{k=n}^{d}\binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k}t^{d-k}\\ &=\sum_{k=0}^{d-n}\binom{n-1+k}{k}t^{k}+\sum_{k=d-n+1}^{d}\binom{d}{k}t^{k}.\end{split}

This shows that products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} spans SkS_{k} for 0⩽k⩽d−n0\leqslant k\leqslant d-n, and the elements of products⁡(F)k\products(F)_{k} are linearly independent for d−n+1⩽k⩽dd-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant d. Observe that at k=d−n+1k=d-n+1, (n−1+kk)=(dk)\binom{n-1+k}{k}=\binom{d}{k}, so products⁡(F)d−n+1\products(F)_{d-n+1} also spans Sd−n+1S_{d-n+1}. ∎

Remark 3.9.

Corollary 3.1 of [2] is essentially the same as Proposition 3.1 of [39], but the proof in [2] is characteristic-independent. The fact that Products⁡(F)k\Products(F)_{k} equals SkS_{k} for k⩽d−n+1k\leqslant d-n+1 also follows from Theorem 5.1 of [2]. Alternatively, the spanning part of the statement follows from [38, Theorem 3.1], which is established by code-theoretic methods. The linear independence part, for d−n+1⩽k⩽dd-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant d, follows by computing the Hilbert functions of ideals of certain unions of linear subspaces in the intersection lattice of the arrangement [18, Proposition 2.9], which turn out to be the ideals generated by Products⁡(F)k\Products(F)_{k} [33, Theorem 2.3].

3.2. Space of derivatives

Next, we show that Derivs⁡(F)k\Derivs(F)_{k} is equal to Products⁡(F)k\Products(F)_{k} for suitable values of kk.

Recall the following:

Definition 3.10.

For a set of vectors {v1,…,vd}\{v_{1},\dotsc,v_{d}\} representing a matroid on the ground set [d]={1,…,d}[d]=\{1,\dotsc,d\}, a flat of the matroid is a subset Σ⊆[d]\Sigma\subseteq[d] such that if viv_{i} lies in span⁡{vj:j∈Σ}\sspan\{v_{j}:j\in\Sigma\}, then i∈Σi\in\Sigma.

That is, a flat consists of all of the vectors in some fixed linear subspace.

For a hyperplane arrangement with hyperplanes {H1,…,Hd}\{H_{1},\dotsc,H_{d}\} defined by linear forms {ℓ1,…,ℓd}\{\ell_{1},\dotsc,\ell_{d}\}, a flat of the arrangement is a flat of the set of vectors {ℓ1,…,ℓd}\{\ell_{1},\dotsc,\ell_{d}\}. Equivalently, a subset Σ⊆[d]\Sigma\subseteq[d] is a flat if, whenever HiH_{i} contains the intersection of the hyperplanes HjH_{j} for j∈Σj\in\Sigma, we also have i∈Σi\in\Sigma. This means a flat of an arrangement consists of all of the hyperplanes in the arrangement that contain some fixed linear subspace.

Lemma 3.11.

Let the ground field have characteristic zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arbitrary arrangement with equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. If Σ⊆[d]\Sigma\subseteq[d] is a flat of the arrangement, then ∏i∈Σℓi∈Derivs⁡(F)\prod_{i\in\Sigma}\ell_{i}\in\Derivs(F).

We give two proofs of the lemma. The first one is under the assumption that the ground field is infinite, which allows us to avoid choosing coordinates. The second one works in general, but involves coordinate choices.

Proof of Lemma 3.11 for infinite base field.

For each ii let HiH_{i} be the hyperplane defined by ℓi=0\ell_{i}=0. Let WW be the intersection of the HiH_{i} for i∈Σi\in\Sigma. The hypothesis that Σ\Sigma is a flat means that W⊆HiW\subseteq H_{i} if and only if i∈Σi\in\Sigma. The infinitude of the ground field ensures that WW is not covered by the union of the finitely many proper subspaces W∩HjW\cap H_{j} for j∉Σj\notin\Sigma, so there is some α∈W\alpha\in W such that α∉Hj\alpha\notin H_{j} for j∉Σj\notin\Sigma.

Since α∈W\alpha\in W, α  ℓi=ℓi​(α)=0\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\ell_{i}=\ell_{i}(\alpha)=0 for all i∈Si\in S. Thus α  (∏i∈Sℓi)=0\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\left(\prod_{i\in S}\ell_{i}\right)=0 by Equation (2.8a). Hence

αd−|Σ| F\displaystyle\alpha^{d-|\Sigma|}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F =αd−|Σ| {(∏i∈Σℓi)⋅(∏j∉Σℓj)}\displaystyle=\alpha^{d-|\Sigma|}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\left\{\left(\prod_{i\in\Sigma}\ell_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{j\notin\Sigma}\ell_{j}\right)\right\}
=(∏i∈Σℓi)⋅{αd−|Σ| (∏j∉Σℓj)}\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{i\in\Sigma}\ell_{i}\right)\cdot\left\{\alpha^{d-|\Sigma|}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\left(\prod_{j\notin\Sigma}\ell_{j}\right)\right\} by (2.8b)
